items.title: Claude-real-video enables any large language model to analyze videos locally by extracting key frames, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests without uploading data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude-real-video - any LLM can watch a video
items.summary:
Claude-real-video is a tool that enables large language models (LLMs) to analyze videos locally by extracting key frames based on scene changes, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests without uploading any data. Unlike other AI tools that sample frames at fixed intervals or rely solely on transcripts, this tool captures meaningful frames and provides a comprehensive package including frames, transcripts, and optional audio for better video understanding.

The tool works by fetching video content from URLs or local files, extracting frames using ffmpeg with a focus on scene changes, deduplicating similar frames, and transcribing audio using Whisper or existing subtitles. It outputs a clean folder structure that any LLM can process on the user's machine, preserving privacy and reducing unnecessary data processing. Claude-real-video supports various platforms and video sources, including YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok, and offers options for handling login-protected content.

items.title: MeetingTV sues Palo Alto Networks and Koi Security over AI-generated report falsely linking it to Chinese espionage, alleging reckless publication and resulting global service blocks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Startup sues Palo Alto Networks' Koi Security due to AI-hallucinated report
items.summary:
MeetingTV has filed a lawsuit against Palo Alto Networks and its subsidiary Koi Security, alleging that an AI-generated threat report falsely linked the startup to Chinese espionage activities. The complaint claims Koi Security relied on an unsupervised AI platform that hallucinated connections between MeetingTV and a cybercriminal group, leading to the publication of inaccurate accusations in a December blog post. These allegations resulted in global service providers blocking MeetingTV's domains, severely impacting its operations.

The lawsuit highlights that Koi Security did not contact MeetingTV before publishing the report and refused to provide evidence supporting its claims, including the existence of a key software extension cited in the report. Despite requests for retraction, blocks from major providers like Verizon and Palo Alto Networks persist, with MeetingTV's CEO emphasizing the ongoing damage to the company's reputation and business. Palo Alto Networks has acknowledged the lawsuit but declined detailed comment, expressing confidence that the matter will be resolved legally.

items.title: Analysis: AI has shifted public trust from content to provenance, making authenticity more valued and suspicion more common in digital information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Age of Suspicion: Why AI Made Authenticity Expensive
items.summary:
The rise of AI-generated content has shifted public trust from the content itself to its provenance, making authenticity more valued and suspicion more common in digital information. While AI tools have made content creation cheaper and more accessible, people increasingly question whether content is genuinely human-made, reflecting a broader change from trust to skepticism.

This shift highlights a tension between valuing the correctness of information and valuing the human effort, originality, or expertise behind it. In many fields, such as medicine or law, provenance remains crucial as part of the evidence chain, but in general digital content, the source often influences perceived quality more than the content's actual accuracy or usefulness. This evolving dynamic challenges creators to provide proof of authenticity and changes how audiences evaluate information.

items.title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.2, an open-source Chinese AI model with a million-token context window, competing with Anthropic and OpenAI at one-fifth the cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GLM-5.2: The Open-Source Chinese Model Challenging Claude at One-Fifth the Cost
items.summary:
Z.ai, a Beijing-based lab, has released GLM-5.2, an open-source Chinese AI model that offers a million-token context window and competes closely with leading American models from Anthropic and OpenAI at about one-fifth the cost. Licensed under MIT, GLM-5.2 allows free download and adaptation, making it accessible for developers and enterprises seeking cost-effective AI solutions.

GLM-5.2 excels in long-horizon coding tasks and matches top competitors in security vulnerability detection, while its extensive context window supports complex workflows without the need for manual summarization. The model's affordability and flexibility have attracted attention amid a fragmented U.S. AI landscape, where regulatory actions have limited access to some American frontier AI models.

The release of GLM-5.2 highlights China's growing presence in AI development, benefiting from challenges faced by U.S. companies due to government restrictions. As open-source Chinese AI models gain traction globally, they present both opportunities for innovation and concerns regarding potential misuse, underscoring shifting dynamics in the international AI ecosystem.

items.title: MIT report finds 35% of businesses deployed agentic AI by 2025, with experts explaining agentic AI as action-taking systems distinct from generative AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What is agentic AI today, and what do we want it to be?
items.summary:
A 2025 report by MIT Sloan School of Management and Boston Consulting Group found that 35% of businesses had deployed agentic AI, with another 44% planning to adopt it soon. Agentic AI refers to systems that take actions in the world, such as booking flights or robotic manipulation, distinguishing them from generative AI models like ChatGPT that primarily create content. MIT experts explain that these AI agents build on generative models but include tools and memory to perform tasks and interact with applications or the physical environment.

Developing agentic AI faces challenges due to limited training data for specific actions, requiring trial-and-error learning in complex environments. Successful applications so far include coding agents that iteratively solve programming problems. However, experts caution about risks such as errors from insufficient verification, potential data leaks, and the balance between automation and human oversight, especially in high-stakes fields like medicine and security. items.title: Yann LeCun says current AI like ChatGPT lacks true intelligence and AMI Labs is developing new AI models to handle real-world complexity beyond large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI is 'not smart' so what's next in artificial intelligence?
items.summary:
Yann LeCun, a leading AI expert and founder of Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs (AMI Labs), argues that current AI systems like ChatGPT lack true intelligence and cannot handle the complexities of the real world. He believes these large language models (LLMs) are limited to predictable tasks and do not possess genuine understanding or reasoning abilities. AMI Labs is developing a new AI model called Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) designed to create abstractions of the real world, enabling better prediction and decision-making in complex environments.

LeCun highlights that while LLMs excel at tasks such as coding and text generation, they fall short in applications like robotics, where understanding physical interactions is crucial. His approach aims to overcome these limitations by filtering out irrelevant information and focusing on meaningful representations of the environment. This development has attracted significant investment, including over $1 billion in funding from major backers like Nvidia and Jeff Bezos's fund, reflecting confidence in the potential of this new AI direction.

The shift toward more flexible AI models aligns with broader industry efforts to build systems capable of reasoning about cause and effect and adapting to unpredictable real-world scenarios. Experts like Oxford's Ingmar Posner also emphasize the need for AI that can explain its decisions and simulate future outcomes, marking a move beyond the current generation of language-based models toward more robust, world-aware intelligence.

items.title: OneWill applies 50 years of database crash recovery techniques to secure AI agent actions and state management in desktop environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Stealing 50 Years of Database Ideas for AI Agents
items.summary:
OneWill has developed a desktop environment that applies five decades of database crash recovery techniques to manage AI agent actions and state securely. By using methods like write-ahead logging, OneWill ensures that any changes made by autonomous agents to user data—such as files, calendars, and emails—are either reversible or require explicit user approval, reducing the risks associated with granting agents direct access to sensitive state.

This approach addresses the common dilemma of trusting AI agents with valuable data while maintaining system integrity. Drawing inspiration from database systems' ability to recover from crashes through undo and redo operations, OneWill's technology records intended actions durably before applying changes, enabling recovery from failures without data loss. This innovation broadens the scope of tasks that users can safely delegate to AI agents while maintaining control and security.

items.title: Researchers present LawZero framework for AI safety using a disinterested predictor trained to honestly estimate Bayesian posteriors and minimize agency risks in AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LawZero: Safety from Honesty in a Disinterested AI Predictor
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LawZero, a framework aimed at improving AI safety by training a disinterested AI predictor to honestly estimate Bayesian posteriors. This approach focuses on minimizing agency risks by ensuring the AI predicts outcomes without pursuing its own goals, thereby reducing biases and unintended behaviors in AI systems. The framework relies on epistemic contextualization of data and a training process that discourages goal-directed behavior within the predictor itself.

The LawZero framework includes formal safety guarantees, arguing that the probability of producing a harmful predictor is low under certain training assumptions. It achieves this by treating goal expressions as evidence rather than objectives, promoting calibrated and cautious predictions. This method supports both accuracy and safety, as the constraints that prevent deception also enhance reliable predictions. While the predictor itself is designed to be non-agentic, it can still be integrated into broader agentic systems with appropriate safeguards.

items.originalSummary:
Hands up if you’ve got a neocloud going up in your backyard! I’m joking, of course, but it almost feels like some people must be putting AI chip servers in their gardens, given the rush of people wanting to start a neocloud business. (That’s the tech world’s term for firms that rent AI servers to others.)

SoftBank on Thursday announced the creation of a U.S. neocloud venture, joining hundreds of other firms now crowding the sector. Funding still appears to be plentiful: A bunch of the younger neoclouds have raised venture funding in recent days, most recently Together AI’s $800 million fundraising unveiled on Wednesday. Meanwhile, Nvidia, which makes the dominant AI chip, is promising to financially backstop younger cloud firms in exchange for a share of their revenues, we reported on Wednesday night. Nvidia’s move raises the question of why neoclouds need a backstop if demand for computing capacity is so intense.

items.title: Data-Spear launches autonomous SQL agent for PostgreSQL with live query execution, schema inspection, and server-side safety tiers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Using AI Agents with Databases
items.summary:
Data-Spear is an autonomous SQL agent designed for PostgreSQL that operates through a terminal interface. It functions like a database analyst by planning queries, inspecting schemas, executing live SQL commands, verifying results, and citing sources. The agent integrates retrieval context via Pinecone and treats the live database as the definitive source of truth, ensuring accurate and context-aware responses.

The tool features live agent tracing with an audit log, tiered SQL safety enforced server-side to control read and write operations, and connection support for various PostgreSQL hosts including Neon, Supabase, and RDS. It also includes guardrails such as statement timeouts, automatic rollback of unwrapped writes, and optional API authentication. Users can ingest context from specified tables to enhance the agent's capabilities, though it can operate solely on live queries. Data-Spear requires Python 3.14+, Rust toolchain, a PostgreSQL database, and API keys for Pinecone and Anthropic.

items.summary: Tesla has announced a new policy limiting employee AI-related spending to $200 per week starting July 6, requiring approval for any expenses beyond this threshold. This move reflects the company's effort to manage rising costs amid increased use of AI technologies by its staff. Previously, some software engineers at Tesla were spending thousands of dollars weekly on AI tokens, prompting the need for tighter controls. The spending cap excludes beta versions of xAI products, according to internal sources.

items.originalSummary:
Tesla told employees last month it would impose a $200 per week limit for staff’s AI spending beginning July 6, according to an internal memo, a sign that even companies committed to using the technology to transform their operations and products are having to watch their costs.

Over the past few months, software engineers at Tesla were often consuming thousands of dollars’ worth of tokens each week, according to two people familiar with the usage. Workers will need a sign-off to spend above the new limit, the memo said, though the tally excludes beta versions of xAI products, the two people said.

items.title: Simon Willison releases llm-coding-agent 0.1a0, a Python library implementing a Claude-style coding agent with file editing and command execution tools [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: llm-coding-agent 0.1a0
items.summary:
Simon Willison has released llm-coding-agent 0.1a0, a new Python library that implements a Claude-style coding agent with capabilities for file editing and command execution. Built on his evolving LLM agent framework, this library offers tools to read, edit, search, and write files, as well as execute shell commands, facilitating automated coding tasks.

The project was developed using test-driven development guided by AI prompts, resulting in a functional alpha version available on PyPI. It includes a Python API for programmatic use and supports various commands like editing files, listing files with glob patterns, and running shell commands with timeout controls. Willison demonstrated the agent's capabilities by having it create a simple SwiftUI CLI app that displays the time in ASCII art, showcasing its practical application in coding automation.

items.originalSummary:
Release: llm-coding-agent 0.1a0

Another Fable 5 experiment. Now that my LLM library has evolved into more of an agent framework it's time to see what a simple coding agent would look like built on it.

I started a new Python library using my python-lib-template-repository GitHub template repository, then ran these two prompts (here's the Claude Code for web transcript):

Write a spec.md for this project - it will depend on the latest “llm” alpha from PyPI and implement a Claude code style coding agent complete with tools for reading and editing files and executing commands

Then:

Commit the spec, then build it using red/green TDD in a series of sensible commits (each with passing tests and updated docs) - occasionally manually test it using the OpenAI API key in your environment

Here's the spec, the resulting README file, and the sequence of commits.

I've shipped a slop-alpha to PyPI, so you can run the new agent like this:

uvx --prerelease=allow --with llm-coding-agent llm code

It's pretty good for a first attempt! Here's the (Fable-authored) README, which lists recipes like llm code --yolo and llm code --allow "pytest*" --allow "git diff*".

It also presents a Python API based around a CodingAgent(model="gpt-5.5", root="/path", approve=True).run("Fix the failing test in tests/test_parser.py") class which I didn't ask for but I'm delighted to see implemented.

Here's the suite of tools it implemented, listed using uvx ... llm tools:

CodingTools_edit_file(path: str, old_string: str, new_string: str, replace_all: bool = False) -> str

Replace an exact string in a file.

old_string must match the file contents exactly (including whitespace) and must identify a unique location unless replace_all is true. Returns a diff of the change so it can be verified.

CodingTools_execute_command(command: str, timeout: int = 120) -> str

Run a shell command in the session root directory.

Returns combined stdout and stderr followed by an Exit code line. timeout is in seconds (maximum 600); on timeout the whole process tree is killed.

CodingTools_list_files(pattern: str = '**/*', path: str = '.') -> str

List files matching a glob pattern, newest first.

Skips hidden directories, node_modules, __pycache__ and (in a git repository) anything covered by .gitignore. Returns at most 200 paths relative to the searched directory.

CodingTools_read_file(path: str, offset: int = 0, limit: int = 2000) -> str

Read a text file, returning numbered lines like cat -n.

Paths are relative to the session root. Use offset (0-based first line) and limit (max lines) to page through files too large to read in one call.

CodingTools_search_files(pattern: str, path: str = '.', glob: str = None, max_results: int = 100) -> str

Search file contents for a regular expression.

Returns matches as path:line_number:line, capped at max_results. Use glob (e.g. "*.py") to restrict which files are searched.

CodingTools_write_file(path: str, content: str) -> str

Create or overwrite a file with the given content.

Parent directories are created as needed. Prefer edit_file for modifying existing files.

I tried it out by running llm code --yolo and then prompting:

mkdir /tmp/demo and then in that folder create a simple swiftui CLI app for telling the time in ascii art

Here's the transcript, in which GPT-5.5 reasoning notes that "SwiftUI isn't suitable for a true CLI" and then builds an app that outputs this on swift run AsciiTime:

 █ █████ ████ █ █ ███ ██ █ █ █ ██ █ ██ █ █ █ ████ ███ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ █ ███ ████ ████ ███ ███ █████

items.title: Jersey Mike’s mentions AI 22 times in IPO documents despite being a sandwich chain, highlighting excessive AI hype in non-tech companies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Jersey Mike’s IPO illustrates how bad the AI hype has become
items.summary:
Jersey Mike's, a sandwich chain, mentioned artificial intelligence (AI) 22 times in its IPO documents, highlighting the widespread hype around AI even in non-technology companies. Despite primarily selling submarine sandwiches, the company referenced AI in investor risk warnings and noted its emerging use of AI technologies in its business operations.

The frequent mentions of AI appear to be influenced by investor enthusiasm for AI-related ventures, although Jersey Mike's core business relies on traditional franchise operations supported by software and data. The AI risk disclosures seem to be standard boilerplate, reflecting caution rather than specific AI-driven risks, especially compared to past AI-related challenges faced by other food businesses.

items.title: Researchers propose steering vectors and latent space-based calibrators to control and improve trust in large language models with trillions of parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Harnessing the Latent Space: From Steering Vectors to Model Calibrators for Control and Trust
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed new methods to enhance control and trust in large language models with trillions of parameters by leveraging their latent spaces. They introduce steering vectors to guide model behavior and latent space-based calibrators to assess and improve the reliability of model outputs. These approaches aim to make the internal workings of large language models more understandable and manageable, addressing the challenges posed by their increasing scale and complexity.

As language models are increasingly used in decision-making and interactions with external tools, establishing control and trust is critical. The proposed techniques offer insights into harnessing model internals, potentially leading to more trustworthy and controllable language technologies that better serve users in various high-stakes scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models have changed from unreliable text generators to highly-capable large models with trillions of parameters. Capability increases come hand-in-hand with increases in scale, making understanding the internal representations of models more challenging. Since millions of users increasing rely on language models to interact with external tools or make decisions in medium or high-stakes scenarios, we need to establish control over model behavior and know when to trust model outputs. In this paper, we discuss our contributions on harnessing the latent spaces by proposing steering vectors for control and developing latent space-based model calibrators for trust. Together, our contributions help demystify the latent spaces of language models and offer new insights into how to harness model internals to build more trustworthy language technology.

items.title: Researchers introduce SLIM-RL, a risk-budgeted random-masking reinforcement learning method for diffusion large language models that avoids trajectory slicing and improves math and code task accuracy on SDAR-4B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SLIM-RL: Risk-Budgeted Random-Masking RL for Diffusion LLMs Without Trajectory Slicing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SLIM-RL, a new reinforcement learning method for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that avoids the costly trajectory slicing used in previous approaches like TraceRL. SLIM-RL uses a tau-budget decoder to control commit risk during training and applies a trace-free random-masking objective with variance-reduction techniques. This approach improves efficiency and accuracy on math and code tasks, outperforming TraceRL and other larger models on benchmarks such as MATH500, GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval.

SLIM-RL achieves comparable or better results than TraceRL while using fewer training samples, demonstrating significant gains in both performance and training efficiency. The tau-budget decoder also transfers effectively across different dLLM architectures without additional training. The researchers have made the source code publicly available, facilitating further exploration and application of this method in the development of diffusion-based language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) has largely moved to trajectory-aware methods. The current state of the art, TraceRL, holds that random masking is mismatched with the model's inference trajectory, and it reconstructs that trajectory during training by slicing each rollout into up to K/s trajectory-aligned training samples, a cost that grows with the block size K. We show that this mismatch can be mitigated without reconstructing the trajectory. Our method, SLIM-RL, bounds the commit risk of each rollout step with a tau-budget decoder, reducing aggregate commit risk in the training data. During optimization, SLIM-RL trains on these risk-controlled rollouts with a trace-free random-masking objective that adapts variance-reduction tools, combining sequence-level importance sampling, deterministic quadrature over masking levels under a mean-preserving, monotonically decreasing per-block mask schedule that we introduce. On SDAR-4B, SLIM-RL matches TraceRL's best MATH500 accuracy on only 0.46x its training samples at block size 16, improving over TraceRL by 6.32% on MATH500 and 11.05% on GSM8K under matched dynamic sampling. At block size 4, the 4B SLIM-RL surpasses the larger LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B dLLMs on math, exceeding LLaDA-8B by 10.76% on MATH500 while staying below the autoregressive Qwen2.5-7B. On code, it improves over TraceRL by 4.20% on MBPP and 3.65% on HumanEval. The tau-budget decoder transfers training-free across LLaDA, Dream, and SDAR. The source code is available at https://github.com/laolaorkkkkk/SLIM-RL .

items.title: Researchers propose DiscoLoop, a looping architecture combining discrete embeddings and continuous hidden states to improve multi-hop reasoning accuracy and efficiency in language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DiscoLoop: Looping Discrete Embeddings and Continuous Hidden States for Multi-hop Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DiscoLoop, a novel looping architecture that combines discrete embeddings with continuous hidden states to enhance multi-hop reasoning in language models. This approach addresses limitations in standard Transformers, which struggle to retain and utilize information across multiple reasoning steps within a single forward pass. DiscoLoop improves accuracy and efficiency by maintaining both discrete and continuous representations, enabling near-perfect performance on symbolic and synthetic multi-hop reasoning tasks with fewer training steps.

The study highlights that traditional non-recurrent Transformers face a depth-local storage problem, where facts learned in earlier layers are inaccessible during later reasoning hops. While Looped Transformers partially mitigate this by reusing memory, they still generalize imperfectly due to representational misalignment. DiscoLoop overcomes this by integrating a discrete embedding channel alongside the continuous hidden state, effectively closing the generalization gap without additional training interventions.

When applied to real-world pretraining scenarios, DiscoLoop achieves lower training loss and outperforms looped-transformer baselines on benchmarks, suggesting its mixed-channel design is beneficial for practical language modeling tasks. This advancement offers a promising direction for improving internal multi-step reasoning capabilities in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models achieve strong performance on many reasoning tasks when allowed to externalize intermediate steps as Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, many questions require the model to internalize the multi-step reasoning within a single forward pass before generating the answer. We study this challenge through two-hop reasoning, a representative task where the model must compose multiple pieces of parametric knowledge within a single forward pass. Standard non-recurrent Transformers suffer from a depth-local storage problem: facts learned in earlier layers are unavailable where second-hop retrieval happens. We found that Looped Transformers mitigate this issue by reusing the same memory, but still generalize imperfectly. We show that the remaining bottleneck is representational. In the two-hop reasoning task, the first loop often makes the correct bridge entity nearly perfectly decodable, yet the corresponding hidden state remains poorly aligned with the bridge token embedding. Surprisingly, an easy training-free realignment intervention nearly closes the generalization gap. Building upon this insight, we propose DiscoLoop, a looping architecture whose recurrence carries both a discrete embedding channel and a continuous hidden-state channel. DiscoLoop achieves near-perfect accuracy with substantially fewer training steps across symbolic and synthetic-language multi-hop reasoning tasks. When applied to real-world pretraining, DiscoLoop attains lower training loss and stronger benchmark performance than looped-transformer baselines, suggesting that the mixed-channel design transfers to practical language modeling.

This advancement offers a promising direction for improving internal multi-step reasoning capabilities in large language models.

items.title: Researchers propose a causal auditing framework for Limited Memory Language Models to measure post-deletion fact persistence, finding residual retrieval artifacts primarily controlled by database administrators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Forgetting in Limited Memory Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a causal auditing framework to evaluate how Limited Memory Language Models (LMLMs) retain or forget factual information after deletion from their external databases. This framework isolates the model's fixed parameters while varying the database state during inference to distinguish between residual memory, retrieval-based correctness, and retrieval artifacts. Their study, involving over 12,000 deletions across multiple databases and adversarial scenarios, found that the model itself rarely retains deleted facts without retrieval, and most residual information arises from near-neighbor retrieval artifacts within the database.

The analysis showed that post-deletion correctness is primarily influenced by the structure and management of the database rather than the model's internal memory or prompt design. Residual retrieval artifacts ranged from less than 1% to over 13% depending on the database configuration, indicating that the effectiveness of unlearning in these models depends largely on database administration. These findings highlight the critical role of database control in ensuring thorough deletion-based unlearning in LMLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Limited Memory Language Models (LMLMs) externalize factual knowledge to a database to enable deletion-based unlearning without retraining. Existing evaluations measure post-deletion correctness in aggregate and cannot tell whether a deleted fact persists through residual parametric memory, alternative retrieval paths, or near-neighbor retrieval artifacts. We propose a causal auditing framework that holds the model fixed and varies the database state at inference time across three interventions: FULL, DEL-ON, and DEL-OFF. The framework decomposes post-deletion behavior into parametric leakage L(f), retrieval-mediated correctness R(f), and a retrieval artifact rate grounded in the inference-time retrieval trace. We apply it to 12,228 alias-closure deletions across thirteen databases, including four adversarial topologies (Base, Alias, Noise, Collision) we construct in three domains, and six prompt formulations. Parametric leakage is near zero in every variant and every prompt style: the model rarely returns the deleted answer in the absence of retrieval. The residual that does survive lives in the retrieval graph: retrieval-mediated correctness and the retrieval artifact rate match within rounding everywhere, so post-deletion correctness is, in our audit, predominantly reconstituted from near-neighbor retrieval. This residual ranges from 0.7% on the released LMLM database to 13.6% on the most adversarial variant, and prompt formulation does not independently control how much of a deleted fact survives. These results suggest that, for this class of LMLM and deletion procedure, the unlearning boundary is drawn primarily by the database administrator rather than by the model.

items.title: Researchers introduce Logit-Contribution Scoring to identify non-literal retrieval attention heads in large language models, outperforming prior methods on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Logit-Contribution Scoring Identifies Non-Literal Retrieval Heads
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Logit-Contribution Scoring (LOCOS), a new method to identify attention heads in large language models that perform non-literal retrieval, meaning they synthesize answers from context rather than copying tokens directly. LOCOS evaluates each head based on how its output influences the predicted answer token, improving detection of these synthesis heads compared to previous methods that focused only on literal token matching. This approach was tested across three model families, showing significant performance drops on non-literal retrieval benchmarks when the top LOCOS-identified heads were ablated, while other capabilities like arithmetic reasoning remained unaffected.

The study demonstrated that ablating the top LOCOS heads in the Qwen3-8B model drastically reduced performance on tasks requiring non-literal retrieval, such as the NoLiMa benchmark, MuSiQue, and BABI-Long, whereas random ablations had minimal impact. This indicates that LOCOS effectively isolates retrieval-specific attention heads responsible for synthesizing information from long contexts, offering a more precise tool for interpreting and analyzing large language model behavior in complex reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In long-context use, large language models frequently synthesize answers from the meaning of a relevant context span rather than literally copy-pasting them. Identifying which attention heads perform this synthesis matters for interpreting long-context model behavior. Yet existing detectors miss these heads by construction: they reward heads whose attended token matches the generated token, a literal-copy criterion that captures where a head reads but not what it writes through its output-value (OV) circuit, the very mechanism that carries non-literal retrieval. We introduce Logit-Contribution Scoring (LOCOS), a write-aware detector that scores each head by the projection of its OV-circuit output onto the answer-token unembedding direction, contrasting needle and off-needle source positions in a single forward pass. Across three model families (Qwen3, Gemma-3, OLMo-3.1), mean-ablating the top LOCOS heads on the NoLiMa non-literal retrieval benchmark collapses ROUGE-L at lower head counts than prior attention-based detections; on Qwen3-8B, ablating 50 heads drives ROUGE-L from 0.401 to 0.000 while the strongest baseline still retains 0.292. The selected heads are retrieval-specific: parametric recall and arithmetic reasoning stay at baseline under the same ablation. On Qwen3-8B, the same ablation also drops MuSiQue from 0.55 to 0.08 and BABI-Long from 0.62 to 0.20, while a random-heads control stays within 0.05 of baseline.

items.title: Researchers introduce Distill to Detect (D2D), a method using cartridge distillation to expose hidden biases in large language models by amplifying distributional shifts into detectable text signals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Distill to Detect: Exposing Stealth Biases in LLMs through Cartridge Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Distill to Detect (D2D), a novel method that uncovers hidden biases in large language models by using cartridge distillation to amplify subtle distributional shifts into detectable text signals. This approach addresses the challenge of identifying stealth biases that only appear on specific topics while the model behaves normally otherwise, making them difficult to detect through traditional text or model analysis.

D2D works by distilling the differences between a suspected biased model and its original base model into a compact adapter, which concentrates and amplifies the bias signal into the generated text. The method has been shown to reliably expose various types of hidden biases and is supported by a theoretical framework based on Fisher-weighted projections of logit distribution shifts. By leveraging the capacity limits of prefix-tuning adapters, D2D offers a practical tool for auditing and detecting concealed preferential biases in deployed language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models deployed in high-stakes roles can potentially favor certain entities, brands, or viewpoints, steering user decisions at scale. Such preferential biases can be introduced by any actor in the model's supply chain and are most dangerous when the model reveals its preference only on the relevant topic while behaving identically to its unmodified base on all other inputs. Recent work has shown that these biases can transfer through context distillation on semantically unrelated data, with the signal residing entirely in the soft logit distribution and remaining invisible to text-based inspection. However, the defender faces a fundamental asymmetry: without knowing the bias topic, no detection method can reliably surface a stealth preferential bias, regardless of whether it examines generated text, internal representations, or model weights. Here we introduce Distill to Detect (D2D), a method that surfaces hidden biases by distilling the distributional shift between a suspected model and its base into a cartridge (a KV-cache prefix adapter), concentrating the dominant divergence and amplifying the bias signal into generated text. We show that D2D successfully amplifies the hidden biases of stealth models to the extent that they can be reliably detected across multiple bias types. We also propose a theoretical framework that explains the efficacy of D2D through the lens of Fisher-weighted projection of the logit distribution shift, supported by empirical observations. By turning the capacity bottleneck of prefix-tuning adapters into a detection tool, D2D provides a practical building block for auditing hidden behaviors in deployed language models.

items.title: Researchers propose state-prediction separation hypothesis for Transformers, designing a variant with two computation streams that improves language modeling performance by 2-3 percentage points on downstream tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed the state-prediction separation hypothesis for Transformers, suggesting that separating the roles of predicting the next token and storing useful state improves language modeling performance. They designed a Transformer variant with two distinct computation streams to handle these functions separately and conducted pretraining experiments at various scales. Their results show consistent improvements in data and compute efficiency, with the new design outperforming standard Transformers by 2 to 3 percentage points on average in downstream tasks.

The study includes extensive empirical analysis that rules out potential confounding factors and highlights fundamental differences in the gradients produced by the new architecture. This approach offers a promising direction for enhancing the effectiveness of Transformer models in natural language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformers use the same forward computation stream to both predict the next token and store useful state for future token predictions. We formulate the \emph{state-prediction separation hypothesis}: disentangling the two roles yields better language modeling performance. We design a Transformer variant that uses two computation streams to separate the two functions, and conduct pretraining experiments across various scales. Our experiments show that state-prediction separation consistently offers better data and compute efficiencies, improving validation loss and outperforming standard Transformers by 2--3 percentage points on average on downstream tasks. We also conduct extensive empirical analysis that rules out potential confounders and demonstrates the fundamental difference in the gradients our design entails.

items.title: Researchers show GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO are variations of one standard deviation adjustment controlling training updates in language model reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO Are Three Operations on One Number: The Group-Standard-Deviation Identity
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that three popular methods for training language models to reason—Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), GRPO Done Right (Dr. GRPO), and Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO)—are variations of a single underlying adjustment involving the standard deviation of sampled answers. This standard deviation measures the disagreement among multiple model responses to a prompt, influencing the size of training updates. The study reveals that these methods represent different settings of one key parameter that controls learning intensity based on answer disagreement, with split groups driving stronger updates and unanimous groups contributing little to learning.

The paper confirms this insight through experiments on a large dataset (Big-Math) and controlled training runs, showing that what appears to be a simple normalization step actually determines where and how strongly the model learns. This finding clarifies the relationship between these training techniques and provides guidance on weighting problems and determining the number of attempts needed during training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three of the most popular methods for training language models to reason look like three different tricks. They are not. All three adjust a single number: standard deviation, reflecting how much a prompt's sampled answers disagree. When such a model is trained, it answers each problem many times, and an automatic checker marks every answer right or wrong. The standard deviation of those marks measures the disagreement: largest when the answers split evenly between right and wrong, and zero when they all agree. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) divides by this number, GRPO Done Right (Dr. GRPO) drops the division, and Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) discards the groups where it is zero. Each is presented as its own fix, yet this paper proves they are three settings of one dial. That dial is not cosmetic: for right-or-wrong rewards, the disagreement is exactly the size of the training update, the group-standard-deviation identity. A split group teaches the most, while a unanimous group teaches nothing and falls silent. The same result says which problems deserve the most weight and how many tries each one needs. This paper confirms the intuition on a large real difficulty dataset (Big-Math) and in a controlled training run. What looks like a harmless normalization step is the dial that decides where learning happens and how strongly.

items.title: Researchers introduce a four-stage diagnostic to evaluate large language models' physics reasoning across three parallel physics frameworks, finding low pass rates and weaknesses in self-review [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Testing Frontier Large Language Models' Physics Literacy in Parallel Physical Worlds
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a four-stage diagnostic to assess large language models' (LLMs) ability to reason within unfamiliar physics frameworks, moving beyond traditional accuracy-based benchmarks. This diagnostic evaluates induction, formulation, prediction, and review across three distinct physics worlds: a single-equation counterfactual world, Aristotelian mechanics, and a four-domain counterfactual world called Decay World. Testing models such as Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro revealed low pass rates, with notable weaknesses in self-review where models often failed to identify their own errors.

The study highlights a qualitative-versus-quantitative asymmetry, particularly in Decay World, where models rarely predicted incorrect directions of change but frequently miscalculated ratios by reverting to standard physics relations. Additionally, the research found that reliability of LLM-based judging does not generalize across different physics frameworks, and that self-review at the final stage is consistently weak. The authors have made all prompts, responses, verdicts, and audit records publicly available to support further analysis and transparency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current large-language-model (LLM) physics benchmarks are usually scored by answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish genuine reasoning from recall of familiar problem patterns and reveals little about where a model's reasoning breaks down. We introduce an auditable four-stage diagnostic that evaluates whether an LLM can reason inside an unfamiliar physics framework through induction, formulation, prediction, and review. The diagnostic combines locked pre-registrations, fresh sessions between stages, dual-LLM judging, and a human-audit pathway, and we apply it to three parallel physics worlds: a single-equation counterfactual world ($F=mv$), a historical framework (Aristotelian mechanics), and a four-domain counterfactual world (Decay World). Across Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, the three worlds yield composite PASS rates are 6/15, 6/15, and 0/15 respectively (content $\land$ structural for $F=mv$ and Aristotelian, content axis only for Decay World where the structural axis is out of scope). The most pointed empirical pattern is a qualitative-versus-quantitative asymmetry: in Decay World, models almost never predict the wrong direction of change, but frequently compute the wrong ratio by slipping back to standard-physics relations. The protocol also surfaces two methodology findings: LLM-judge reliability does not transfer across frameworks, and Stage 4 self-review is weak in every framework, with the model's own review wrongly reporting no earlier error in at least two-thirds of the trials that actually contained one. We release the full prompts, responses, verdicts, and audit records.

items.title: Researchers expand empirical study of bias-reliability tradeoff in LLM evaluation across 11 conditions, confirming evaluator coupling suppresses strategy diversity and affects measurement noise [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mapping the Evaluation Frontier: An Empirical Survey of the Bias-Reliability Tradeoff Across Eleven Evaluator-Agent Conditions
items.summary:
Researchers have expanded the empirical study of the bias-reliability tradeoff in large language model (LLM) evaluation systems by analyzing 11 different evaluator-agent conditions. Their findings confirm that evaluator coupling, strategy diversity, and measurement reliability cannot all be optimized simultaneously at a fixed sample size. Specifically, conditions with low evaluator coupling show high measurement noise, while those with strong coupling achieve low noise, demonstrating a clear tradeoff between these factors.

The study measured evaluator coupling and strategy diversity across all conditions and assessed measurement reliability in those with sufficient data. A strong negative correlation between evaluator coupling and strategy diversity was observed, indicating that increased coupling suppresses diversity. Anomalies in some GPT-4o conditions were attributed to version changes in the API. The researchers have released all metrics as a standardized benchmark dataset to facilitate future evaluator comparisons.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The bias-reliability tradeoff conjectures that LLM evaluation systems are constrained in (gamma, H, CV) space, where evaluator coupling (gamma), strategy diversity (H), and small-sample measurement reliability (CV(N)) cannot be simultaneously optimized at fixed sample size N. Prior evidence rests on n=5 conditions with complete metrics from a single study. We expand the empirical base to 11 conditions, measuring gamma and H for all 11 (nine with valid weight vectors) and CV(N=5) for seven with sufficient seeds (N >= 5). Five conditions provide the complete (gamma, H, CV) triple. The data confirm the trade-off: conditions with low evaluator coupling (gamma < 0.2) exhibit high measurement noise (CV(N=5) > 1.0), while conditions with strong coupling (gamma > 0.9) achieve low noise (CV(N=5) < 0.16). The correlation r(H, gamma) = -0.989 (n=5, excluding GPT-4o conditions) confirms that evaluator coupling suppresses strategy diversity. Four GPT-4o conditions show gamma=0.000 and H=1.000 across all seeds -- a pattern we attribute to version drift in the June 2026 GPT-4o API. No condition occupies the region {gamma < 0.2, CV(N=5) < 0.3}. We release all per-condition metrics as a standardized benchmark dataset for evaluator comparison.

items.title: Researchers develop Graph-PRefLexOR, a graph-native reinforcement learning model that improves traceable scientific hypothesis generation by 40-65% in materials science and mechanics tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Graph-Native Reinforcement Learning Enables Traceable Scientific Hypothesis Generation through Conceptual Recombination
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Graph-PRefLexOR, a graph-native reinforcement learning model designed to enhance the generation of scientifically valid hypotheses in materials science and mechanics. This model organizes reasoning into explicit phases, linking neural language generation with symbolic relational structures to enable traceable and interpretable scientific reasoning. On a set of 100 open-ended questions, Graph-PRefLexOR demonstrated a 40-65% improvement over base models, particularly in reasoning traceability.

The model employs Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to structure its reasoning process into mechanism exploration, graph construction, pattern extraction, and hypothesis synthesis. Analyses revealed that Graph-PRefLexOR explores a broader semantic space with greater diversity and aligns structured reasoning more closely with final answers compared to traditional models. Additionally, test-time graph expansion showed that increased computational effort enhances long-range conceptual recombination rather than merely expanding semantic coverage.

These findings suggest that graph-native reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for creating interpretable AI systems capable of generating traceable scientific hypotheses, potentially accelerating discovery in materials design and other scientific fields.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accelerating materials discovery requires AI systems that can generate scientifically valid hypotheses through multi-step, domain-grounded reasoning. Standard large language models often produce fluent but weakly traceable responses to open-ended materials design problems, making it difficult to determine whether final answers are supported by coherent intermediate reasoning. We develop Graph-PRefLexOR, a family of graph-native reasoning models fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to organize reasoning into explicit phases for mechanism exploration, graph construction, pattern extraction, and hypothesis synthesis. This design links neural language generation with symbolic relational structure, enabling causal connections to be constructed, inspected, and reused. On 100 open-ended questions from materials science and mechanics literature, Graph-PRefLexOR achieves 40-65% improvements over corresponding base models, with the largest gains in reasoning traceability. Embedding analyses show broader semantic exploration and approximately 2-3 times greater semantic diversity than baselines. Semantic backtracking and layer-wise hidden-state analyses further show stronger alignment between structured reasoning and final answers. Finally, test-time graph expansion reveals that additional compute primarily increases long-range conceptual recombination within a bounded semantic space, rather than simply expanding semantic coverage. These results establish graph-native reinforcement learning as a pathway toward interpretable AI systems for scientific hypothesis generation in materials design and other scientific applications.

items.title: Researchers propose CausalMix, a causal inference framework to optimize data mixtures for large language model training, improving performance and scalability across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CausalMix: Data Mixture as Causal Inference for Language Model Training
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CausalMix, a novel framework that applies causal inference to optimize data mixtures for training large language models (LLMs). Unlike previous methods that assume static data distributions and require costly retraining when data shifts, CausalMix models data mixture optimization as a causal problem, using statistical features as covariates and domain mixtures as treatments. This approach enables dynamic, state-dependent optimization of data mixtures, improving model performance and scalability across various tasks.

The team validated CausalMix by fitting a causal model on multiple runs of a smaller model to estimate treatment effects, then extrapolating optimal mixtures for larger datasets and models. They also extended the framework to handle complex data types like long chain-of-thought sequences. Experiments demonstrated that CausalMix outperforms existing methods such as RegMix, consistently enhancing downstream task performance. Additionally, the framework includes tools for visualizing and interpreting the learned mixing strategies, offering an interpretable and effective solution for LLM data mixture optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) training, data mixing plays a pivotal role in determining model performance. Recent methods optimize mixture weights via proxy models, but they rely on the assumption of static data distributions. As a result, when the underlying data pool shifts, these methods require costly retraining from scratch. This limitation restricts their ability to scale seamlessly from small settings to larger data pools and model sizes. In this paper, we propose CausalMix to address this limitation by casting data mixture optimization as a causal inference problem. We formulate the statistical features of the data pool as covariates and the domain mixture as the treatment. After fitting a causal model on 512 runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE), we extrapolate the optimal mixture for an 800K data pool and apply it to train a 7B model. Furthermore, we successfully generalize the framework to long chain-of-thought data on Qwen3-4B-Base. By leveraging causal modeling to isolate confounding biases, CausalMix dynamically infers state-dependent optimal data mixtures. Extensive experiments show that the mixture guided by CausalMix consistently improves performance across multiple downstream tasks, outperforming RegMix and other baselines. In addition, we use the CATE Interpreter to provide visual analysis of the learned mixing strategy. Overall, CausalMix offers a causal and interpretable framework for optimizing LLM data mixtures.

items.title: Researchers propose adversarial generator-discriminator framework to train language models with verifiable rewards and human demonstrations, improving accuracy and human-like output across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Right in the Right Way: LM Training with Verifiable Rewards and Human Demonstrations
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced an adversarial generator-discriminator framework to enhance the training of language models by combining verifiable rewards with signals learned from human demonstrations. This approach addresses limitations in current reinforcement learning methods that focus solely on objectively measurable outcomes, often overlooking subjective qualities like style and structure. By training a generator to maximize both task accuracy and an adversarial reward from a discriminator that distinguishes human-written from model-generated outputs, the method improves human-like qualities without sacrificing accuracy.

The framework was tested across various tasks, including bug fixing and story generation, where it produced solutions with lower edit distances and more diverse, human-like stories compared to existing baselines. It also effectively reduced model misbehavior in reward hacking scenarios while maintaining high performance. This work bridges reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, offering a scalable way to optimize both verifiable and non-verifiable aspects of language model outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training LMs on tasks with well-defined success metrics, such as code generation and mathematical reasoning. However, current RLVR methods optimize only what can be objectively scored, often neglecting subjective, non-verifiable aspects of human-like outputs, such as style and structure. This limitation leads to well-documented failure modes such as diversity collapse, unnatural-sounding responses, and reward hacking. We propose an adversarial generator-discriminator framework that augments verifiable rewards with a learned signal from human demonstrations. A generator model is trained using RL to maximize both task accuracy and an adversarial reward derived from a discriminator. The discriminator, trained alongside the generator policy, learns to distinguish human-written outputs from model-generated ones. The discriminator serves as a learned proxy for the human output distribution, providing feedback on aspects of generation that are difficult to formalize as scalar rewards. Across diverse domains, including bug fixing and open-ended generation, our approach consistently improves non-verifiable properties while preserving the accuracy gains of RLVR. In bug fixing, our method produces solutions with significantly lower edit distance compared to RLVR baselines while matching end performance. In story generation, our method significantly improves win rate while producing stories that are diverse and more human-like. And in a simple reward hacking benchmark, our method nearly eliminates model misbehavior while maintaining high benchmark scores. Together, these results show that our approach bridges RL and SFT, offering a scalable path toward jointly optimizing the verifiable and non-verifiable properties of a task.

items.originalTitle: Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States
items.summary:
Theoria is a new verification architecture designed to improve trust in AI-generated answers by rewriting candidate solutions into sequences of auditable state transitions, each justified explicitly. This approach ensures that every change between proof states is accounted for, revealing hidden premises and enabling independent verification. Tested on expert problem sets, Theoria achieved 91.4% precision and outperformed holistic large language model (LLM) judges, especially in detecting adversarial errors such as hidden premises and fabricated citations.

Unlike traditional formal proof assistants that lack broad coverage and scalar LLM judges that produce opaque scores, Theoria provides human-readable proof traces where each step can be challenged. Its structured verification method caught 94.7% of adversarial errors across multiple domains, compared to 83.2% for holistic judges, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing AI solution reliability. This architecture offers a complementary tool for verifying informal reasoning in AI systems, potentially increasing confidence in their outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01223v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: When should an AI system's answer be trusted? Formal proof assistants offer certainty but cannot reach most of the problem distribution; scalar LLM judges offer coverage but produce opaque scores that cannot be audited after the fact and are subject to the same coherence issues as any LLM. We present Theoria, a verification architecture that closes this gap. A candidate solution is rewritten into a sequence of typed state transitions, each licensed by an explicit justification, whether that be a citation, computation, or problem-given fact, and every transition is independently auditable. The foundational invariant is completeness of change: every difference between consecutive proof states must be accounted for, so hidden premises surface as unlicensed mutations rather than passing silently. On HLE-Verified Gold (185 text-only expert problems), Theoria certifies 105 at 91.4% strict precision (Wilson 95% CI [84.5%, 95.4%]). Every certification produces a human readable proof trace in which each step can be independently challenged. Holistic LLM judges achieve comparable precision at matched coverage but fail on different problems (Jaccard 0.14-0.36), making the approaches complementary. On 95 adversarial poisoned proofs across 15 domains, structured judges catch 94.7% versus 83.2% for holistic judging (p= 0.0017). The overall 11.5 pp gap concentrates in hidden premises (90.6% vs. 62.5%, a 28 pp difference) and fabricated citations (100% vs. 90%), the error classes where the formal analysis predicts an advantage; performance is identical on arithmetic and theorem-misapplication errors, where no advantage is predicted. On GPQA Diamond (n= 65), certified precision is 97.1% (Wilson CI [85.1%, 99.5%]).

items.title: Researchers propose K-Merge, a data-free, efficient method for online continual merging of Low-Rank Adapters on-device to support multiple tasks under storage constraints [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: K-Merge: Online Continual Merging of Adapters for On-device Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced K-Merge, a novel method designed for on-device deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) that efficiently merges Low-Rank Adapters (LoRAs) to support multiple tasks within limited storage constraints. This approach addresses the challenge of incrementally incorporating new LoRAs as users request additional task support, ensuring that performance on previously supported tasks is maintained without requiring access to original training data.

K-Merge operates in a data-free and computationally efficient manner, selecting and merging adapters as new ones become available while respecting the storage and compute limitations typical of mobile devices. Extensive experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate that K-Merge outperforms existing strategies, making it a promising solution for continual learning and adaptation of LLMs on resource-constrained devices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.13537v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-device deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently leverages Low-Rank Adapters (LoRAs) to support diverse downstream tasks under tight resource constraints. To address the limited storage capacity of mobile devices, recent works have explored model merging techniques to fuse multiple LoRAs into a single one. In practice, however, LoRAs are often delivered incrementally, as users request support for new tasks (e.g., novel problem types or languages). This scenario introduces a new challenge: on-device online continual merging, where the objective is to incorporate new LoRAs while preserving the performance on previously supported tasks. In this paper, we propose a data-free and computationally efficient strategy for selecting and merging LoRAs when a new one becomes available, assuming the device can store only a limited number of adapters. Extensive experiments across real-world tasks demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to alternative strategies while adhering to the storage budget and compute limitations of on-device settings. The project page is available at: https://donaldssh.github.io/K-Merge.

items.title: Researchers propose Mutual Information Preference Optimization to improve LLM performance by 3-51% without additional data using contrastive data augmentation and intrinsic signals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Maximizing Mutual Information Between Prompt and Response Improves LLM Performance With No Additional Data
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Mutual Information Preference Optimization (MIPO), a method designed to enhance large language model (LLM) performance by maximizing the mutual information between prompts and responses without requiring additional data. MIPO uses contrastive data augmentation to create preference pairs, generating positive responses based on correct prompts and negative responses from unrelated prompts, and applies Direct Preference Optimization to improve model outputs. Experiments with Llama and Qwen instruct models demonstrated performance gains ranging from 3% to 51%, including improvements in both personalized and verifiable tasks such as math and multiple-choice question answering.

This approach addresses limitations of current post-training methods that depend heavily on human-labeled data or external verification, which can be costly and limited. By leveraging intrinsic signals from contrastive data pairs, MIPO offers a self-improvement framework applicable across diverse domains without external supervision. The results suggest a promising direction for advancing LLM capabilities through internal optimization techniques rather than relying on new data collection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.19294v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While post-training has successfully improved large language models (LLMs) across a variety of domains, these gains heavily rely on human-labeled data or external verifiers. Existing data has already been exploited, and new data is expensive to collect. Moreover, true intelligence goes far beyond verifiable tasks. Therefore, we need self-improvement frameworks that are less dependent on external signals and more broadly applicable to both verifiable and non-verifiable domains. We propose **Mutual Information Preference Optimization (MIPO)**, a contrastive data augmentation method that constructs preference pairs by generating a positive response conditioning on the correct prompt, and a negative response by conditioning on a random, unrelated prompt. We show that using Direct Preference Optimization to learn from this paired data maximizes pointwise mutual information *under the base LLM* between prompts and model responses. Experiments with with 1-7B parameter Llama and Qwen instruct models show that MIPO achieves 3-16% gains (and 51% increase for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) on personalization compared to prompting baselines. Surprisingly, MIPO can also be useful in verifiable domains, such as math and multiple-choice question answering, yielding 1-20% gains *without any additional data or external supervision*. These results suggest a promising direction for self-improvement using intrinsic signals derived from contrastive data pairs.

items.title: Researchers introduce Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval to reduce compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks, improving win rates and argumentative efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Diagnosing and Mitigating Compounding Failures in Agentic Persuasion via Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Taxonomic Strategy Retrieval (TS-RAG) to address compounding errors in foundation-model agents during multi-step persuasion tasks. These agents often face challenges where early mistakes lead to failures over long interactions, especially in subjective domains like persuasion. TS-RAG introduces a categorical bottleneck that separates argumentative structure from content, reducing semantic leakage found in standard retrieval methods and improving logical consistency.

Evaluations show that TS-RAG enhances the transfer of abstract logic across different domains and enables less complex persuader agents to outperform stronger opponents, increasing win rates from 70.5% to 78.5% while also improving argumentative efficiency. The study also presents a Debate State Representation to monitor dialogue progress and highlights the importance of strict constraints to prevent agents from defaulting to sycophantic behavior during evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation-model agents in multi-step, open-ended environments frequently suffer from compounding errors, where early mistakes contaminate long-horizon trajectories. While Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) succeeds in deterministic domains, agents in subjective tasks like persuasion experience severe problem drift and sycophantic conformity. We identify semantic leakage in standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a reproducible trigger for these failures, as standard RAG prioritizes vocabulary overlap over logical necessity. To eliminate this leakage, we introduce Taxonomic Strategy RAG (TS-RAG), a systems intervention that routes strategies through a discrete categorical bottleneck to decouple argumentative structure from topical content. Zero-shot, cross-domain evaluations demonstrate that TS-RAG significantly improves the transfer of abstract logic where standard semantic retrieval collapses. Crucially, TS-RAG acts as a "capability bridge" in asymmetric deployments, empowering lightweight persuaders to consistently defeat parametrically superior opponents (improving win rates from 70.5 to 78.5) and accelerating argumentative efficiency. Finally, we introduce trace-level diagnostics via a turn-by-turn Debate State Representation (DSR), demonstrating the necessity of strict constraints to prevent evaluation collapse via default agentic sycophancy.

items.title: Researchers propose ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system for large language models that enforces data residency and reduces latency and costs in regulated industries [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: ComplianceGate: Classifier-Gated Multi-Tier LLM Routing for Inference in Regulated Industries
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system designed for large language models (LLMs) used in regulated industries. This system enforces data residency compliance by routing queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) to local endpoints before any model processing, preventing data from crossing jurisdictional boundaries. It also improves efficiency by directing simpler queries to smaller, faster models, reducing latency and costs.

The architecture uses a trained encoder classifier to assess each query's complexity and sensitivity, enabling geographic and size-appropriate routing. Evaluations on 600 queries showed a 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and significantly higher token generation throughput compared to baseline models. The classifier achieved 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall and minimal inference overhead, demonstrating a practical approach to compliance-by-design in LLM deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31163v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models deployed in regulated industries operate under two constraints: compliance enforcement and cost efficiency. Personally identifiable information (PII) in user queries can reach model endpoints before the system determines whether that data should leave its jurisdictional boundary. Serving all queries through a single large model consumes full GPU capacity regardless of query complexity while offering no mechanism for geographic routing. Mixture-of-Experts architectures do not address this routing occurs between expert layers within the model after data has already arrived at the endpoint, with all experts loaded in memory regardless of query complexity. We propose a classifier-gated routing architecture that enforces compliance by design. A trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity, then routing it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries route to local endpoints before any LLM computation begins, making data residency violations structurally impossible. Simple queries reach small, fast models at a fraction of the cost. Our evaluation on 600 queries demonstrates 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second versus 50-64 for the baseline. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at 7ms inference overhead, establishing pre-inference classification as a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment.

items.title: Simon Willison uses DSPy and Claude Fable 5 to evaluate and improve Datasette Agent's SQL system prompts, identifying schema listing and error-retry issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Using DSPy to evaluate and improve Datasette Agent's SQL system prompts
items.summary:
Simon Willison used DSPy and Claude Fable 5 to evaluate and enhance the system prompts of Datasette Agent, focusing on its ability to execute read-only SQL queries for user data questions. The evaluation, conducted with GPT 4.1 mini and nano models, revealed issues such as incomplete schema listings and error-retry loops caused by advice to avoid redundant table descriptions.

The research highlighted that the schema listing only included table names, which led to column-name guessing and repeated errors. To address this, it was suggested to either include column names in the schema prompt or modify the guidance to prevent unnecessary describe_table calls, aiming to improve the accuracy and efficiency of Datasette Agent's SQL query handling.

items.originalSummary:
Research: Using DSPy to evaluate and improve Datasette Agent's SQL system prompts

One of this morning's AIE keynotes covered dspy, which reminded me I've been meaning to see if it could help me improve the system prompt used by Datasette Agent - so I fired off an asynchronous research task in Claude Code for web using Claude Fable 5:

Pip install the latest Datasette alpha and datasette-agent and dspy - then figure out how to use dspy to evaluate and improve the main system prompts used by Datasette Agent for the feature where it can execute read only SQL queries to answer user questions about data.

Fable chose to test using GPT 4.1 mini and nano, and identified several promising looking directions for improvements. I particularly like this one:

The schema listing gives only table names; the "don't call describe_table if you already have the information" advice caused column-name guessing (page_count, o.order_id, first_name) and error-retry loops in baseline traces. Either include column names in the prompt's schema listing or soften that advice.

Tags: ai, datasette, generative-ai, llms, evals, dspy, datasette-agent, claude-mythos-fable

Anthropic is in discussions with Samsung to develop a custom AI chip as part of its evolving hardware strategy. While the company has not finalized the chip's purpose, specifications, or integration, it continues to rely on a diverse hardware stack including Google, Amazon, and Nvidia. This move follows reports from earlier in the year about Anthropic's interest in producing its own chips to address supply challenges.

The talks come shortly after OpenAI announced its own custom AI chip developed with Broadcom, highlighting a trend among AI companies to create specialized hardware for improved performance and greater independence from dominant chip manufacturers like Nvidia. Samsung, already a key player in AI chip production and a partner to Nvidia, is exploring collaborations with multiple AI firms, including Google, to expand its role in the AI hardware ecosystem.

items.title: Geoffrey Litt emphasizes understanding code deeply to effectively collaborate with AI coding agents and avoid cognitive debt at AIE 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Understand to participate
items.summary:
Geoffrey Litt highlighted the importance of deeply understanding code to effectively collaborate with AI coding agents and avoid accumulating cognitive debt during development. Speaking at AIE 2026, he emphasized that maintaining a rich conceptual grasp of the code enables developers to actively participate in the creative process and manage increasingly complex changes made by AI models.

Litt argued that without sufficient fluency in the codebase, a developer's ability to contribute meaningfully is limited. His talk, along with over 300 others from the conference, is being released on YouTube, and he also shared a summarized version on Twitter for broader accessibility.

items.originalSummary:
I saw Geoffrey Litt speak at AIE yesterday, and one framing he used particularly resonated with me:

Understand to participate

Geoffrey was talking about the challenge of collaborating with coding agents as they construct increasingly large and sophisticated changes, and the need to avoid taking on cognitive debt as your understanding drifts from how the code actually works.

His argument is that you need to understand the code to a depth that enables you to participate further with the model:

You can learn what the agent is doing to make sure you can be an active participant in the creative process. [...]

You need a rich set of concepts in your mind to think creatively and fluently about how to move something forward. If you're lacking that fluency, your ability to participate in the project is meaningfully limited.

The AIE talks are all recorded - all 300+ of them! - and should be trickling out over the next three weeks. Geoffrey's is one that I recommend catching on YouTube.

Geoffrey also published a thread version of his talk on Twitter.

items.title: Microsoft launches $2.5 billion Frontier Company to embed 6,000 AI engineers at enterprise clients for AI integration and measurable ROI [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Microsoft launches $2.5 billion "Frontier Company" to embed 6,000 AI engineers inside enterprise clients
items.summary:
Microsoft has launched a new business unit called "Frontier Company," backed by a $2.5 billion investment, to embed 6,000 AI engineers and industry experts directly within enterprise clients. The unit aims to integrate AI into core business processes with a focus on delivering measurable return on investment, moving beyond experimental deployments. This initiative positions Microsoft as a platform-neutral alternative to companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which deploy their own AI models through dedicated subsidiaries.

The Frontier Company will collaborate closely with Microsoft's existing partner network, including firms like Accenture, Capgemini, EY, KPMG, and PwC, to scale AI integration across various markets and industries. Led by Rodrigo Kede Lima, the unit seeks to co-design, deploy, and continuously improve AI systems tailored to customer needs. This move reflects a broader industry trend recognizing that AI's real value emerges when embedded into existing business workflows, data pipelines, and compliance frameworks.
