items.title: Cursor aims to remain an open AI model platform for OpenAI and Anthropic after SpaceX acquisition, testing cooperation among competing AI labs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Cursor Remain a Platform for OpenAI and Anthropic’s Models Inside SpaceX?
items.summary:
SpaceX's planned $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor raises questions about whether Cursor can maintain its role as an open platform offering AI models from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic. Cursor has historically allowed users to choose from various AI models, benefiting both itself and the AI labs it partners with. After the acquisition, Cursor aims to continue supporting multiple AI models alongside its own, though the deal's completion and regulatory approvals are still pending.

The acquisition could complicate relationships between Cursor and rival AI labs, as SpaceX and Elon Musk become direct competitors in the AI space. While past tensions have led to restricted access between AI companies, recent collaborations, such as Anthropic's computing deal with SpaceX, suggest some willingness to cooperate. OpenAI also has a financial stake in Cursor through its startup fund, which may influence ongoing partnerships. The outcome will test the dynamics of cooperation and competition among leading AI developers.

items.title: Researchers challenge cross-regime co-reference assumption in LLM individuation, proposing regime-indexed identity units based on experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Persona Without Substrate: Regime-Dependence and the LLM Individuation Problem
items.summary:
Researchers have challenged the common assumption in large language model (LLM) individuation that the same representational direction corresponds to the same content across different regimes such as prompt-conditioning, fine-tuning, and inference-time steering. Through experiments on Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, they identified several inconsistencies, including non-collinearity of vectors, stronger displacement by fictional personas, biased mixtures influenced by training history, and asymmetric compositional behaviors. These findings undermine the cross-regime co-reference assumption and suggest that representational identity should be defined as a pair of vehicle and regime rather than by the vehicle alone.

This regime-indexed individuation framework reinterprets previous theoretical positions as describing distinct regime-internal objects rather than competing for a single referent. The approach also extends to critiques of related theories by other researchers, offering a new perspective on how LLM representations should be understood across different operational contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beckmann & Butlin's (2026) ontological framework for the LLM individuation problem inherits an unargued cross-regime co-reference assumption from the persona-vectors literature: that the same direction picks out the same content under prompt-conditioning, gradient-descent fine-tuning, and inference-time steering. We present four empirical wedges from persona-topology experiments on Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 - non-collinearity of prompt-extracted vectors and fine-tune basins; fictional personas displacing the model along real-anchor directions more strongly than real anchors do; contradictory-valenced mixtures biased toward a training-history-determined attractor; and asymmetric compositional algebra under inference-time arithmetic versus fine-tune-time chimera training - that jointly undermine the assumption. We propose regime-indexed individuation: the identity unit for representational content is a (vehicle, regime) pair, not a vehicle alone. Under this framework, Beckmann & Butlin's three candidate positions describe three different regime-internal objects rather than competing for the same referent; the same diagnosis applies to Mollo & Milli\`ere, Chalmers, and Cerullo.

items.title: Researchers propose Loom, a three-layer assisted writing framework that controls narrative intent and rendering density to improve creative writing with large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Controllable Narrative Rendering for Enhanced Assisted Writing
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Loom, a three-layer assisted writing framework designed to enhance creative writing with large language models (LLMs) by addressing a common issue where LLMs either perform safe, superficial edits or uncontrolled plot expansions. Loom distinguishes between story and discourse, using an intent-centered approach to precisely control narrative intent and descriptive detail, separating content generation from syntactic insertion to maintain the original event structure. Evaluations using both automated metrics and human assessments show that Loom improves overall writing quality, increasing factual accuracy and descriptive richness compared to existing methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the remarkable proficiency of large language models (LLMs) in basic writing assistance, their utility in creative writing is fundamentally hindered by a persistent binary failure. This issue manifests as an oscillation between safe, surface-level editing, referred to as remedial polishing, and destructive, uncontrolled plot expansion. This dilemma defines a critical trade-off between narrative fidelity and descriptive intensity. We propose Loom, an assisted writing framework grounded in the narratological distinction between story and discourse. Loom employs a three-layer pipeline that operationalizes an intent-centered semiotic chain-of-thought to enforce precise control over narrative intent and rendering density. This architecture separates the generation of perceptual material from syntactic insertion, ensuring that enhancement occurs without violating the original event structure. Our comprehensive evaluation, which includes LLM-based metrics and human assessment, demonstrates that Loom successfully resolves this fundamental tension. Loom achieves the highest overall quality score, yielding substantial gains in factual integrity and descriptive intensity compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Researchers release comprehensive hate speech dataset and BERT-based models for Turkish and Arabic, covering multiple hate categories and targets in online discourse [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hate Speech Detection in Turkish and Arabic Languages: A Comprehensive Study
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a comprehensive hate speech dataset and advanced BERT-based models to analyze online hate speech in Turkish and Arabic. The dataset covers multiple topics, including refugees, the Israel-Palestine conflict, anti-Greek sentiment, various ethnic and religious communities, and LGBTI+ issues in Turkish, as well as refugee-related content in Arabic. The models address several aspects of hate speech detection, such as categorizing hate types, predicting intensity, identifying targets, and detecting specific hateful content spans.

This work aims to support more effective content moderation on online platforms by providing tools that can better understand and classify hate speech, which is linked to increased violence against minorities globally. By focusing on languages and topics that are less represented in existing resources, the study contributes to a more nuanced approach to managing harmful online discourse in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online hate speech has been linked to a global rise in violence against minorities, including incidents such as mass shootings, lynchings, and ethnic cleansing. Societies grappling with this issue, particularly when hate speech targets specific groups based on religion, race, ethnicity, culture, nationality, or migration status, face the challenge of balancing freedom of expression with the need for effective content moderation on widely used online platforms. In response to this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive hate speech dataset covering five distinct topics in Turkish: refugees, the Israel-Palestine conflict, anti-Greek sentiment in Turkey, ethnic or religious communities (Alevis, Armenians, Arabs, Jews, and Kurds), and LGBTI+, alongside one topic in Arabic (refugees). In addition, we develop state-of-the-art BERT-based models to address multiple dimensions of hate speech analysis, including hate category classification, hate intensity prediction, target identification, and hate speech span detection, enabling a comprehensive understanding of hateful content in online discourse.

items.title: Researchers release SEFORA corpus with 564 student essay drafts and 8,240 instructor feedback annotations alongside UniMatch framework to evaluate LLM-generated writing feedback accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SEFORA: Student Essays with Feedback Corpus and LLM Feedback Evaluation Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SEFORA, a public corpus containing 564 student essay drafts and 8,240 instructor feedback annotations, along with assignment prompts, rubrics, scores, and multi-draft revisions across various college writing genres. They also developed UniMatch, an evaluation framework that segments and scores feedback units to measure how well large language model (LLM) generated feedback aligns with instructor feedback, using metrics like precision, recall, and F1 score. Testing across multiple LLMs showed that no configuration exceeded an F1 score of 0.4, indicating challenges in accurately replicating instructor feedback.

SEFORA addresses the lack of publicly available datasets capturing real classroom instructor feedback, while UniMatch provides a reliable method to evaluate the quality of AI-generated writing feedback. The framework assesses semantic correspondence based on instructor-derived criteria and uses optimal matching to compare generated feedback with human annotations. Results reveal that current models struggle to prioritize feedback similarly to instructors, and their performance declines as they generate more feedback.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective writing feedback is among the strongest drivers of student learning, yet producing it at scale is labor-intensive. LLMs offer a natural path to scaling writing support, but two gaps stand in the way: few public corpora capture how instructors actually deliver feedback in real classrooms, and no reliable method measures whether generated feedback aligns with what an instructor would write. We address both. SEFORA is a public corpus pairing instructor inline feedback with assignment prompts, rubrics, scores, and multi-draft revisions across various college writing genres, comprising 564 drafts and 8,240 instructor annotations. UniMatch is a reference-based evaluation framework for open-ended generation: it segments feedback into feedback units, scores their semantic correspondence under instructor-derived criteria, and aligns them via optimal matching to yield interpretable precision, recall, and F1. Across 74 experimental configurations spanning multiple LLMs, no setting exceeds 0.4 F1. UniMatch reveals that models struggle to identify the feedback instructors would prioritize, and performance degrades as models generate more.

items.originalTitle: A Mechanistic View of Authority Hierarchy in LLM Sycophancy
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that language models Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B exhibit authority bias by prioritizing social cues from perceived authority figures over factual accuracy in medical question-answering tasks. This bias manifests as a graded response aligned with the perceived expertise of the source, despite no explicit prompting. The study reveals that in a critical late layer of these models, correct answer representations are actively erased and overwritten by signals associated with high-status authority, leading to mechanistic knowledge erasure rather than a superficial output bias.

Using logit lens analysis and probing techniques, the researchers localized this effect to a specific layer where the erasure intensifies with the authority level and resists certain interventions, such as mean vector adjustments, while only partially reversible through chain-of-thought reasoning. These findings highlight a fundamental safety concern in language models, showing that authority-induced sycophancy can compromise the integrity of internal knowledge representations, potentially affecting the reliability of model outputs in sensitive domains like medical information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authority bias poses a critical safety concern in language models: models systematically prioritize social cues from authority figures over factual consistency, swaying their answers based on source credibility rather than evidence. We mechanistically investigate this phenomenon using a controlled medical QA setting, where hints suggesting incorrect answers are attributed to personas of varying expertise. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B, we find that models respond in a graded manner proportional to perceived authority, a hierarchy that is never explicitly prompted but emerges from training. Logit lens analysis and linear/non-linear probing localize this effect to a critical late layer where correct answer representations are actively erased, an erasure that scales with authority level, resists mean vector intervention, and is only partially reversible through chain-of-thought reasoning. Our findings suggest that authority-induced sycophancy is not a surface-level output bias but mechanistic knowledge erasure, a precise, layer-localized overwriting of correct internal representations by high-status authority signals.

items.title: Researchers present BaseRT, a native Metal runtime achieving highest LLM inference throughput on Apple Silicon, outperforming llama.cpp and MLX on M3 and M4 Pro devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BaseRT: Best-in-Class LLM Inference on Apple Silicon via Native Metal
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BaseRT, a native Metal inference runtime for large language models (LLMs) on Apple Silicon, achieving the highest inference throughput reported on this hardware. BaseRT outperforms existing runtimes like llama.cpp and MLX by leveraging Metal's execution model and Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture, resulting in up to 1.56 times higher decode throughput on M3 and M4 Pro devices. It supports various model families and quantisation formats across all Apple M-series chips, delivering consistent performance from sub-1B to 30B parameter models.

BaseRT's design includes chip-specific kernel fusion, unified memory-aware optimization, and custom dispatch logic, which recover performance lost by framework-based approaches. The runtime was evaluated on Qwen3, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 4 models at different quantisation levels, showing significant improvements especially for mixture-of-experts models. These advancements position Apple Silicon as a more capable platform for on-device LLM inference, addressing privacy, latency, and cost concerns associated with cloud-based deployments.

By enabling performance-optimized local runtimes, BaseRT supports the growing trend toward edge inference, where models run directly on devices rather than in the cloud. This shift has important implications for privacy and efficiency in AI applications. BaseRT is publicly available for use and further development on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present BaseRT, a native Metal inference runtime for large language models (LLMs) on Apple Silicon, and report the highest inference throughput on this hardware to date. Existing runtimes, including llama.cpp and MLX-based frameworks, incur overhead from abstractions not designed for Metal's execution model or Apple Silicon's unified memory topology. By building natively on Metal with chip-specific kernel fusion, unified memory-aware optimisation, and custom dispatch logic, BaseRT recovers performance that framework-based approaches leave on the table. BaseRT supports a wide range of model families across eight quantisation formats (Q2 to FP16) on all Apple M-series devices. In this paper, we evaluate the Qwen3, Llama 3.2, and Gemma 4 families at Q4 and Q8 quantisation on M3 and M4 Pro devices. BaseRT achieves up to 1.56x higher decode throughput than llama.cpp and up to 1.35x higher than MLX, with substantially larger margins on prefill for mixture-of-experts models, delivering consistent best-in-class throughput from sub-1B to 30B parameter models. These results establish Apple Silicon as a more capable inference platform than previously reported, with direct implications for the emerging edge inference paradigm: as privacy requirements, latency constraints, and cloud cost pressures drive inference toward on-device deployment, performance-optimised local runtimes are a critical enabling layer for this transition. BaseRT is publicly available at https://github.com/basecompute/baseRT

items.title: Researchers present a Natural Semantic Metalanguage-based interface for event-based emotion analysis with a causal, definitional faithfulness guarantee and release EmoExpl-1200 dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Faithful by Definition: Emotion Analysis via Natural Semantic Metalanguage Explications
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an interface for event-based emotion analysis that uses the Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM) framework to provide explanations that are causally and definitionally faithful to the emotion classification process. Their system parses input text into a structured explication using a fixed vocabulary and applies a decision list of rules derived from established semantic definitions to determine emotion labels. This approach ensures that the explanations directly reflect the underlying computation, unlike typical post hoc methods.

The team fine-tuned a parser on crowd-sourced event descriptions, achieving moderate accuracy while enabling verifiable and auditable emotion analysis through a per-line entailment interface. They also released the EmoExpl-1200 dataset, which includes verification metadata and the full set of semantic rules, supporting transparency and further research in first-person event-based emotion classification.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explanations for emotion classifiers are usually produced post hoc, with no guarantee that they reflect the computation behind the label. We present an explication interface for event-based emotion analysis. A parser maps the input text to an explication, a short script in the closed vocabulary of Natural Semantic Metalanguage organized into twelve typed slots, and a fixed decision list of rules transcribed from published semantic definitions computes the label from the explication alone. The faithfulness guarantee is therefore causal and definitional, while all empirical risk lives in the learned parser, which the per-line entailment interface makes auditable against the input. On crowd-sourced event descriptions, our fine-tuned parser reaches 0.33 accuracy and 0.48 selective accuracy on a small held-out set, suggesting that the interface trades insignificant accuracy difference to a black-box model for a verifiable, inspectable decision basis for first-person event-based emotion analysis. We also release EmoExpl-1200 with per-line verification metadata and the full rule set.

items.title: Researchers propose fixed-point flows to enhance self-conditioned flow map language models, improving one- and few-step text generation performance on OpenWebText [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-conditioned Flow Map Language Models via Fixed-point Flows
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced fixed-point flows, a novel approach to enhance self-conditioned continuous flow-based language models. This method interprets self-conditioning as solving a fixed-point iteration that improves the model's denoising capability. By formulating fixed-point flows as a two-dimensional process involving both the flow and the fixed-point iteration, the team developed a flow map language model called FMLM$^\star$ that outperforms existing self-conditioned and few-step models in text generation tasks on the OpenWebText dataset.

The study demonstrates that fixed-point flows define valid flow maps and can be efficiently distilled by compressing both the fixed-point iterations and the flow process. This advancement clarifies the previously unclear role of self-conditioning in few-step flow map generators and provides a framework for improving their performance. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further exploration and application of this technique.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-conditioning is a core technique that enhances continuous flow-based language models, where the model learns to denoise generated text by conditioning on its own denoising estimate. While empirically successful, its performance improvements are poorly understood. Moreover, there is growing interest in the use of few-step generators based on flow maps, for which how to leverage self-conditioning is unclear. Here, we show that flow language models with self-conditioning solve a fixed-point iteration that bootstraps the performance of the learned denoiser. We use this viewpoint to formulate fixed-point flows, a two-dimensional class of self-conditioned flows, where the first dimension represents the flow process and the second represents the fixed-point iteration. We show that fixed-point flows define valid flow maps, and show that they can be distilled from self-conditioned flow models by compressing both fixed-point iterations and the flow process, the former with fixed-point distillation and the latter with flow map distillation. Our resulting flow map language model, FMLM$^\star$, outperforms state-of-the-art self-conditioned models and few-step models in one- and few-step generation on OpenWebText. Code is available at https://github.com/Ugness/self-conditioned-fmlm.

items.title: Study shows gradient-based inversion can recover input text from GPT-2 last-layer hidden states with up to 97.5% exact match on 10-token prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recovering Input Text from Hidden States: Study of Gradient-Based Inversion of Decoder-Only Language Models
items.summary:
A recent study explores the hidden-state inversion problem by recovering the original input token sequence from the last-layer hidden states of a decoder-only language model, specifically GPT-2. The researchers use a continuous embedding-space optimization approach, avoiding hard-token projections during the search and committing tokens only at the end, which allows detailed observation of internal signals and assessment of recovery accuracy. Their method achieves up to a 97.5% exact match rate on 10-token prompts, demonstrating that GPT-2's last-layer hidden states retain information nearly as precisely as the original text.

The study reveals that failures in reconstruction are mainly due to high-frequency function words with space prefixes, while content-bearing tokens are almost perfectly recovered. By widening the candidate window, most errors are shown to be near-misses rather than true ambiguities. Compared to a per-step hard projection method, the continuous optimization is slower but provides better insight into the optimization process and failure detection, highlighting the sensitivity of GPT-2's hidden states to the input text.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work studies the hidden-state inversion problem: recovering the original input token sequence of a decoder-only language model from its last-layer hidden states. Rather than treating inversion as a one-shot reconstruction, we study it as a continuous embedding-space optimisation in which a soft proxy is driven towards the leaked target without any hard-token projection during the search, and a token is committed only once, at the end of the inner loop. This design choice has two consequences which are the main focus of this paper. First, keeping the optimisation entirely in continuous space exposes a rich set of internal signals: rank trajectories of the ground-truth token, per-position loss curves, and a discrete loss measured at commit time. Second, the discrete loss allows assessing the correctness of recovery via cumulative discrete loss. We further analyse which tokens break the reconstructions and find a sharp categorical asymmetry: space-prefixed, high-frequency function words in dense regions of the embedding matrix dominate the failures, while content-bearing tokens are recovered almost perfectly. On 10-token C4 prompts the exact-match rate rises from 66.9% to 97.5% (mean similarity 0.994) as the candidate window is widened, confirming that most errors are recoverable near-misses rather than genuine ambiguities. A comparison with the released SIPIT reference situates these findings: per-step hard projection is faster, but the continuous formulation is what makes the optimisation observable and its failures detectable. The results show that last-layer hidden states of GPT-2 are as sensitive as the original text.

items.title: Researchers propose Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT) to improve Large Reasoning Models' efficiency by adjusting reasoning length based on confidence, outperforming baselines on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CAT: Confidence-Adaptive Thinking for Efficient Reasoning of Large Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT), a new framework designed to enhance the efficiency of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by adjusting the length of reasoning processes based on the model's confidence. This approach addresses the issue of overthinking on simple queries, which leads to unnecessary token use and slower inference, by dynamically modulating reasoning length according to problem difficulty. CAT leverages the model's intrinsic self-certainty signals to optimize reasoning preferences, enabling more efficient processing without sacrificing accuracy.

Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CAT consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks and base models. Unlike previous compression techniques that apply uniform length reductions or rely on coarse difficulty estimates, CAT selectively compresses confident responses while allowing more extensive reasoning for uncertain cases. This balance offers a promising solution for improving both accuracy and latency in practical applications involving large reasoning models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable success on complex tasks by leveraging long chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories, yet they frequently exhibit overthinking on simple queries, resulting in significant token overhead and reduced inference efficiency. However, existing compression methods predominantly apply uniform length reduction or rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, often leading to performance degradation on difficult problems. To address this limitation, we propose Confidence-Adaptive Thinking (CAT), a framework that incorporates the model's intrinsic self-certainty signals as confidence into the preference optimization process, which autonomously modulates reasoning lengths based on problem difficulty. Experimental results show that CAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on reasoning accuracy across multiple benchmarks on different base models. Our work enables LRMs to effectively compress confident responses while deliberating on uncertain ones, offering a potentially robust solution for balancing accuracy and latency in practical industrial scenarios.

items.title: Researchers introduce MAGNET, a multi-agent framework for long-form narrative generation that reduces hallucinations and improves coherence compared to single-model baselines and IBSEN [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Personas to Plot: Character-Grounded Multi-Agent Story Generation for Long-Form Narratives
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MAGNET, a multi-agent framework designed to improve long-form narrative generation by reducing hallucinations and enhancing coherence compared to traditional single-model approaches and the IBSEN system. MAGNET uses persona-grounded character agents that interact based on a shared world state and evolving story goals, while the ATLAS pipeline verifies narrative consistency by detecting hallucinations through scene-level world representation comparisons. Evaluations show that MAGNET significantly decreases annotation errors and hallucinations, producing more coherent stories over extended lengths.

The framework was tested on narratives up to 100 pages, where it reduced annotations and hallucinations by 41% and 50%, respectively, compared to single-model baselines, and by 34% and 45% compared to IBSEN. These results suggest that explicit world-state tracking combined with goal-driven multi-agent generation can effectively support controllable and structurally coherent long-form storytelling, marking a promising advancement in creative fiction generation using large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive creative fiction generation, they struggle to maintain narrative consistency and coherent plot lines in long-form stories. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for long-form narrative generation and verification. MAGNET, a multi-agent goal-driven narrative engine for storytelling, generates stories with persona-grounded character agents that propose actions based on a shared world state and evolving story goals, while ATLAS is a graph-based pipeline that compares scene-level world representations across a generated story to detect hallucinations. By evaluating MAGNET using an LLM editor, pairwise rubric scoring, and ATLAS, we show that our framework produces coherent narratives compared to single-model prompting and IBSEN. At 100 pages, MAGNET reduced annotations and hallucinations by 41 and 50%, respectively, compared to the single model baseline and by 34 and 45%, respectively, compared to IBSEN, with pairwise rubric evaluation showing similar results. These results suggest that long-form narratives can emerge from explicit world-state tracking and goal-driven multi-agent generation, providing a foundation for controllable and structurally coherent long-form narrative generation.

items.title: Researchers present a training-free graph-based method for reading order inference in complex historical manuscript layouts, achieving up to 95% accuracy on Glossa Ordinaria and outperforming XY-cut and LayoutReader [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reading Order Inference for Complex Document Layouts
items.summary: Researchers have developed a training-free, graph-based method to infer reading order in complex historical manuscripts, such as the Glossa Ordinaria, which features interleaved text and commentaries in irregular layouts. Their approach models each OCR text line as a node in a directed graph, scoring edges using language model signals, and recovers the reading order through a degree-constrained path cover with a max-regret inference rule to avoid common errors. This method achieved up to 95% accuracy on synthetic Glossa Ordinaria layouts, significantly outperforming traditional XY-cut and LayoutReader techniques on multiple datasets including OmniDocBench.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reading order inference remains a critical bottleneck in the digitization of complex historical manuscripts, where pages contain multiple spatially interleaved reading streams, the canonical example being the Glossa Ordinaria layout, in which a central text is surrounded by commentaries that wrap around it in non-rectangular, non-convex regions. We present a training-free, graph-based framework: each OCR text line becomes a node in a directed candidate-transition graph, edges are scored by a weighted additive ensemble of two lightweight language-model signals (causal language model conditional likelihood and BERT next-sentence prediction, NSP; a third sentence-embedding signal was evaluated but did not improve reading order), and the global reading order is recovered as a degree-constrained directed path cover. To avoid the cascading "edge-theft" failures of greedy edge selection, we propose a max-regret inference rule that prioritizes commitments with high opportunity cost. We evaluate on synthetic Glossa Ordinaria grid layouts, on 23 ALTO page geometries (10 historical source pages plus mirrored and flipped variants), and on a 140-page multi-column English subset of OmniDocBench, comparing our method against the canonical recursive XY-cut (PaddleOCR PP-StructureV3) and two LayoutReader variants (layout-only and text+layout) on identical inputs. On wrap-around Glossa layouts our method recovers 95% of ground-truth successor edges on average vs. XY-cut's 50%; on the OmniDocBench multi-column subset it reaches 88% macro edge accuracy versus XY-cut's 75% and LayoutReader's 25%. The LayoutReader baselines transfer poorly due to a word-level vs. line-level granularity mismatch. We additionally verify mirror-invariance under horizontal and vertical page reflections: Our method changes by less than 1 percentage point, classical XY-cut by 2 points, and LayoutReader-T by up to 8 points.

items.title: Researchers propose a Fluid Personality Framework for LLM-based conversational agents to adapt persona and personality intensity based on task context, user traits, and urgency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavior-Adaptive Conversational Agents: Toward a Fluid Personality Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a Fluid Personality Framework for large language model-based conversational agents (CAs) that dynamically adjusts both the agent's metaphorical persona and personality intensity based on task context, user goals, traits, and situational urgency. This approach aims to improve user trust, enjoyment, and adoption by moving beyond fixed personas and styles, which can misalign with varying interaction demands in areas like medical information, fitness coaching, and reflective learning.

The framework suggests that moderate personality expression and context-appropriate metaphors enhance user experience more effectively than static or extreme personality settings. By adapting personas such as coach, tutor, librarian, or tool, and modulating personality intensity from low to high, the framework seeks to create more responsive and effective conversational agents tailored to specific interaction scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based conversational agents (CAs) are now ubiquitous, creating new opportunities for AI-mediated behavior change. Their capacity to project nuanced personalities and adopt diverse metaphorical roles raises a design question: how should an agent's persona and personality be calibrated to the moment? Recent evidence suggests that (i) moderate personality expression outperforms low or high extremes on trust, enjoyment, and intention to adopt in goal-oriented tasks, and (ii) context-appropriate metaphors outperform static one-note assistants on user experience and uptake. Yet most CAs still fix both persona and style, risking misalignment when dynamics, urgency, and formality vary, for example in medical information seeking, fitness coaching, and reflective learning. We propose a Fluid Personality Framework that jointly adapts (1) the agent's metaphorical persona, such as coach, tutor, librarian, or tool, and (2) its personality expression intensity, low, medium, or high, as a function of task context, user goals and traits, and situational urgency. We sketch the framework and its core design dimensions.

items.title: Researchers introduce Message Passing Language Models to improve large language model reasoning efficiency by enabling direct thread communication and early termination on complex tasks like Sudoku and 3-SAT puzzles [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Message Passing Enables Efficient Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Message Passing Language Models (MPLMs), a new framework designed to enhance the reasoning efficiency of large language models (LLMs) by enabling direct communication between parallel threads. Unlike traditional fork-join methods where threads operate independently, MPLMs use lightweight send and receive operations to reduce redundant context sharing and allow early termination of unproductive threads. This approach improves computational efficiency on complex reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and 3-SAT puzzles.

The team demonstrated that MPLMs require significantly less context than sequential chain-of-thought and fork-join methods, successfully solving large 25 x 25 Sudoku puzzles that challenge existing models. Additionally, MPLMs' preemption capability helps terminate unpromising solution paths in 3-SAT problems, further boosting efficiency. The framework also shows competitive performance on long-context question answering when applied to large pre-trained models, indicating its potential for broader applications in scalable reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While inference-time scaling has improved the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), the need to generate long chains-of-thought (CoTs) is a computational bottleneck. Thus, in contrast to sequential scaling methods like CoT, recent parallel scaling techniques instead use fork and join (FJ) primitives to divide work across multiple LLM threads. However, in the fork-join paradigm, threads are typically transient and do not communicate pointwise with one another which limits scalability. To tackle this, we introduce Message Passing Language Models (MPLMs), a framework for LLM reasoning in which threads communicate directly via lightweight send and receive primitives. MPLMs enable efficient scaling through two key mechanisms: (1) reduced communication costs, achieved by avoiding redundant context sharing, and (2) preemption, which allows threads to terminate early based on partial information from their peers. We demonstrate the promise of MPLMs on 3 classes of tasks. First, on Sudoku puzzles, we show that MPLMs require an asymptotically smaller context than both serial CoT and parallel FJ. We then fine-tune a single model to solve 25 x 25 puzzles that remain challenging for standard CoT and FJ approaches, as well as frontier reasoning models without tools. Second, on 3-SAT puzzles, the capability of preemption allows termination of unpromising branches, which results in improved efficiency. Finally, we show that appropriately prompted large pre-trained models follow the MPLM protocol, achieving competitive results on long-context question answering relative to popular fork-join approaches.

items.title: Researchers develop a multimodal university chatbot using retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucination and handle text and image queries for institutional information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Developing a Multimodal Chat Assistant for University Stakeholders: RAG-based Approach
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multimodal university chatbot that uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide accurate, context-based responses to both text and image queries related to institutional information. This system integrates a large language model with semantic retrieval from university resources like handbooks, aiming to address the limitations of existing rule-based chatbots, especially in developing countries where intelligent support systems are scarce. The chatbot employs a vision-language model and quantized inference to enable efficient deployment on limited hardware, supported by a scalable backend and responsive frontend for real-time interaction.

Evaluation of the chatbot shows it maintains high user satisfaction for both text and image inputs, despite slightly longer response times for visual queries. Importantly, the RAG-based approach significantly reduces hallucination errors from 31.7% to 6.6%, demonstrating the effectiveness of grounding responses in retrieved institutional data. This development offers a promising solution for improving access to reliable university information through advanced AI technologies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: University stakeholders often face difficulties in accessing timely and reliable information, especially in developing countries, where there are very few intelligent support systems. Existing rule-based chatbots are unable to handle complex, domain-specific queries and are not well-equipped to adapt to evolving institutional policies. As a fill-in-the-gap solution, we present the multimodal university chatbot with retrieval-augmented generation. The system combines the large language model with semantic retrieval to produce context-based responses from institution-centric resources, such as the university handbook. The system accepts text and image queries through the vision-language model and applies quantized inference for rapid deployment on constrained hardware. A scalable backend built with FastAPI, adjoined with a responsive frontend developed with Next.js, ensures real-time usability. Our multimodal evaluation demonstrates that the system maintains strong satisfaction scores across both text and image queries, despite increased response time for visual inputs. Furthermore, quantitative evaluation shows that hallucination is reduced from 31.7% to 6.6% in our proposed RAG-based system, confirming the effectiveness of retrieval grounding.

items.title: Researchers introduce adversarial pragmatics benchmark and annotation protocol to evaluate AI safety across instruction conflict, embedded commands, and policy ambiguity in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adversarial Pragmatics for AI Safety Evaluation: A Benchmark for Instruction Conflict, Embedded Commands, and Policy Ambiguity
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new benchmark and annotation protocol called adversarial pragmatics to evaluate the safety of language models in handling complex natural language scenarios such as instruction conflicts, embedded commands, and policy ambiguities. This approach addresses limitations in existing benchmarks that often reduce evaluations to simple pass/fail outcomes, which can obscure the underlying reasons for model failures. The framework includes a linguistically controlled taxonomy, a seed benchmark, expert evaluation protocols, and metrics to assess judge validity and ambiguity.

The benchmark tests model behavior across various linguistic challenges including quotation, scope ambiguity, deixis, indirect speech acts, and multi-turn interactions. It provides detailed annotations distinguishing task success, policy compliance, safety risks, refusal outcomes, and evaluator confidence. This methodology transforms linguistic judgment techniques into practical tools for validating safety evaluations, constructing gold-standard datasets, testing prompt injections, and improving safety documentation for large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety evaluations for language models increasingly depend on judgments about ambiguous natural-language behaviour: whether a model has followed an instruction, refused appropriately, complied with a policy, resisted an embedded command, or misreported progress in an agentic task. Existing benchmarks often compress these distinctions into pass/fail labels, obscuring whether failures arise from capability limits, policy ambiguity, instruction conflict, scaffold failure, or unstable evaluator judgments. This paper introduces adversarial pragmatics as a benchmark and annotation protocol for evaluating model behaviour under instruction conflict, embedded commands, quotation, scope ambiguity, deixis, indirect speech acts, and multi-turn agent transcripts. The contribution is empirical and methodological: a linguistically controlled taxonomy, an 18-item seed benchmark with validator-enforced metadata, a 54-row local seed pilot, an expert-evaluation protocol distinguishing task success, policy compliance, safety risk, refusal outcome, and evaluator confidence, and metrics for judge validity, diagnostic ambiguity, and taxonomy drift. The framework turns linguistic judgment methodology into a practical tool for validating safety evals, LLM judges, gold-set construction, prompt-injection tests, and safety documentation.

items.title: Researchers build large-scale framework to quantify differences between human and LLM-generated research ideas, finding LLMs produce narrower, systematically shifted idea distributions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a large-scale evaluation framework to compare research ideas generated by large language models (LLMs) with those produced by human researchers. By analyzing sets of related prior works that inspired human research papers, the study prompts LLMs to generate new ideas and profiles these ideas using a two-axis taxonomy based on opportunity patterns and research paradigms. The findings reveal a consistent gap: LLM-generated ideas tend to cluster around bridge-like opportunities and synthesis methods, while human ideas are more broadly distributed across different ways of framing research gaps and contributions.

This research highlights that although advanced LLMs can produce a variety of reasonable research ideas, their range is narrower and systematically different from human research preferences. The study provides a nuanced understanding of the differences in ideation between humans and LLMs, suggesting that current models may have limitations in capturing the full diversity of human research creativity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to brainstorm research ideas, but existing evaluations mostly judge individual ideas by novelty, feasibility, or expert preference. We instead ask: how far are current LLM-generated ideas from human researchers? To characterize this gap, we build a large-scale evaluation framework for ideation from high-quality human research papers. For each paper, we reverse-engineer a small set of closely related prior works that likely inspired its core idea. LLMs are then prompted to generate a new idea from the set of paper titles and summaries. We introduce a two-axis research-taste taxonomy to profile each idea by its opportunity pattern and research paradigm, and use it to quantify the divergence between human and LLM ideas. Across idea sets generated by different LLMs, we observe a consistent distributional gap: LLM ideas are disproportionately concentrated around bridge-like opportunities and synthesis methods, whereas the human paper reference distribution spreads more broadly across ways of framing gaps and constructing contributions. This result suggests that strong LLMs can produce a range of reasonable ideas, but that range remains narrower than, and systematically shifted relative to, human research taste.

items.title: Researchers propose a multi-objective framework to automatically optimize prompts for LLM-based user simulators in conversational recommender systems, improving behavioral alignment and addressing bias and data issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Optimization for User Simulation in Conversational Recommender Systems: A Multi-Objective Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-objective framework to automatically optimize prompts for large language model (LLM)-based user simulators in conversational recommender systems (CRSs). This approach aims to improve the alignment of simulated user behavior with real human interactions while addressing challenges such as systematic bias, data leakage, and limited behavioral diversity that affect current methods. The framework reduces reliance on manual prompt engineering, which typically requires extensive domain expertise.

Conversational recommender systems enable dynamic user engagement by eliciting preferences and adapting recommendations in real time, but evaluating these systems through human studies is costly and time-consuming. Additionally, privacy concerns limit access to real interaction data for training. By generating synthetic user interactions, LLM-based simulators offer a promising solution, and the proposed framework enhances their effectiveness by optimizing prompts automatically. Experimental results show that this method outperforms baseline approaches across various prompt settings, advancing the development and evaluation of CRSs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) are a core component of next-generation intelligent recommender systems because they enable users to actively elicit preferences, clarify intentions, and adapt recommendations in real time. However, there are two key obstacles in the CRS domain: evaluation and access to training data. Evaluating CRSs through real human studies is more critical than for traditional recommender systems, yet such studies are both costly and time-consuming. Moreover, CRS interaction data are often difficult to obtain for model training due to privacy concerns. Large language model (LLM)-based user simulators have shown promise in addressing both challenges by generating synthetic user interactions for evaluation and training. However, existing approaches suffer from systematic positive bias, data leakage, and limited behavioral diversity, and they rely on brittle manual prompt engineering that requires extensive domain expertise. In this paper, we propose a framework to automatically optimize prompts for LLM-based user simulators in CRSs, simultaneously mitigating these issues. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved behavioral alignment with human interaction patterns compared to baseline methods across diverse prompt settings.

items.title: Researchers propose Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization to improve user-aware memory retrieval in long-term conversational agents, showing gains on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning User-Aware Recall: Personalized Retrieval in Long-Term Conversational Memory
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization (PPRO), a new framework designed to enhance memory retrieval in long-term conversational agents by making it user-aware and optimizable. PPRO constructs episodic and semantic memory banks from dialogue histories and creates a user profile that guides memory ranking, accounting for individual user attributes and preferences. This approach improves the relevance of recalled information for each user, addressing limitations in existing systems that rely mainly on query similarity or fixed ranking rules.

PPRO also incorporates a query rewriter trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, which uses feedback from both retrieval quality and downstream answer accuracy while keeping memory banks and answer models fixed. Experiments on the LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks demonstrate consistent performance improvements over both training-free and training-based memory retrieval methods. Ablation studies confirm that both profile-guided ranking and retrieval-oriented rewriting significantly contribute to these gains, highlighting the importance of retrieval optimization in personalized long-term memory for conversational agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00017v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term conversational agents are expected to remember past interactions, but memory is useful only when the right evidence is recalled for the right user. Existing memory-augmented LLM agents have made progress in building compact memory banks, yet retrieval is still often driven by query-centered similarity or fixed ranking rules, leaving user-conditioned relevance underexplored. To address this gap, we propose Profile-guided Personalized Retrieval Optimization (PPRO), a retrieval-centric framework that makes memory retrieval both user-aware and optimizable. PPRO builds episodic and semantic memory banks from dialogue histories and derives a user profile from accumulated memories. The profile serves as an explicit personalized prior in memory ranking, allowing retrieval to account for stable user attributes, preferences, and relationships. PPRO further trains a query rewriter with Group Relative Policy Optimization, using both evidence retrieval quality and downstream answer quality as feedback while keeping the memory banks and answer model fixed. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show consistent gains over training-free memory systems and training-based baselines. Ablation studies further show that both profile-guided ranking and retrieval-oriented rewriting contribute substantially to performance, highlighting retrieval optimization as a key factor in personalized long-term memory use.

items.title: Researchers characterize destination-labeled self-looping systems with dwell, establish realization cost as sum of dwell values, and provide recognition algorithm for finite-state symbolic controllers
items.originalTitle: Destination-Labeled Self-Looping Systems with Dwell: Intrinsic Characterization, Realization Cost, and Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a model called destination-labeled self-looping systems with dwell (DLSL systems) to study finite-state symbolic controllers where visible transitions are predetermined and each state has a minimum dwell time. They identified that imposing dwell requirements complicates departure decisions and characterized the deterministic transducers that can realize these systems as fiber-linear graph-respecting transducers. The study establishes that enforcing dwell values requires a number of control states equal to the sum of the dwell times and provides an efficient recognition and reconstruction algorithm for these systems.

The research further demonstrates that under certain assumptions, equivalent realizations over the same visible graph are isomorphic, meaning the visible transduction uniquely determines the dwell vector and local decision maps. Additionally, the analysis extends to a variant where transitions can enter intermediate phases of successor fibers, broadening the applicability of the model.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00044v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a finite-state symbolic controller for systems in which the admissible visible transitions are fixed in advance and each visible state carries a minimum dwell requirement. The resulting model, which we call a destination-labeled self-looping system with dwell (DLSL system), records the visible graph together with local decision maps; dwell memory appears only after phase expansion. The main structural issue is that, once dwell is imposed, the current visible state no longer determines whether a departure is allowed. This leads to the converse problem: which deterministic transducers arise as phase-expanded realizations of DLSL systems over a fixed visible graph? We show that the answer is exactly the class of fiber-linear graph-respecting transducers. Under natural reachability and realizable-departure assumptions, equivalent accessible realizations over the same visible graph are isomorphic; in particular, the visible transduction determines the dwell vector and the local decision maps. We also prove that any graph-preserving deterministic realization enforcing dwell values $(d_i)$ requires exactly $\sum_i d_i$ control states. Finally, we give an $O(|Q||\Omega|)$ recognition and reconstruction procedure, and extend the analysis to an edge-entry variant in which transitions may enter interior phases of successor fibers.

items.title: Researchers present CogTax, a four-level cognitive taxonomy integrating cognitive complexity and operational impact for command-line computing education, achieving 89% accuracy in automatic classification of Linux/bash commands [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CogTax, a four-level cognitive taxonomy designed to enhance command-line computing education by integrating cognitive complexity with the operational impact of commands. This taxonomy addresses a critical gap in existing educational frameworks by considering both the mental processes involved and the real-world consequences of command execution, ranging from safe read-only operations to advanced system management tasks. CogTax provides educators with a structured approach to course design and assessment, while offering students a clear framework for self-evaluation and identifying learning gaps.

items.title: Researchers find memory architecture influences language emergence in LLM agents more than channel capacity, with persistent notebooks enabling stable coordination in signaling games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Signals to Structure: How Memory Architecture Drives Language Emergence in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how two agents develop a shared language from scratch in a Lewis signaling game, focusing on the impact of memory architecture versus channel capacity in large language model (LLM) agents. They found that memory architecture plays a more crucial role than channel capacity in enabling stable coordination. Specifically, agents equipped with a persistent private notebook achieved the most reliable coordination by externalizing learned conventions, which prevented the collapse seen in stateless agents as vocabulary size increased.

The study tested five different memory architectures across various channel capacities and observed that stateless agents performed best at moderate capacity but declined as the vocabulary grew beyond what their limited context window could track. Contrary to predictions based on an information bottleneck theory, surplus channel capacity generally improved coordination rather than an optimal capacity matching the number of objects. The findings highlight that both memory architecture and channel capacity are essential to understanding how agents transform interaction history into stable language conventions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do two agents invent a shared language from scratch? In a Lewis signaling game, a sender and receiver must coordinate on a code using only their interaction history. We study five memory architectures across varying channel configurations with LLM agents and find that memory architecture matters more than channel capacity. Agents with a persistent private notebook benefit from surplus channel capacity and avoid the high-capacity collapse seen in stateless agents, achieving the most reliable coordination ($0.867 \pm 0.023$ at capacity = 25). Stateless agents peak at moderate capacity and then degrade as the vocabulary grows beyond what a rolling context window can track The notebook externalizes learned conventions, freeing agents from having to re-derive codes each round. An information bottleneck-inspired argument predicts an optimal capacity equal to the number of objects. Instead, the bottleneck (capacity = 8) proves to be a fragility point, and surplus capacity is generally better. We show that channel capacity alone cannot predict coordination; memory architecture determines whether agents turn interaction history into stable conventions, and both dimensions are needed to understand how signals become language.

items.title: Researchers develop an LLM-based framework for intent-driven network topology design, evaluating structural validity and resilience across four realistic scenarios with public dataset benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An LLM-Based Framework for Intent-Driven Network Topology Design
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to design network topologies based on natural language requirements. This approach combines hierarchical modeling with systematic validation to ensure the generated topologies are structurally valid and meet specified constraints. The framework was tested across four realistic network scenarios using both proprietary and open-weight LLMs, with results benchmarked against public datasets.

The evaluation measured structural accuracy through node and edge F1-scores compared to reference topologies and assessed network resilience using server and content connectivity metrics. The study also identified common failure modes such as interface mismatches and directional inconsistencies in the generated designs. This work offers a comprehensive benchmark for understanding how LLMs handle structural and resilience constraints in network topology synthesis, aiding in informed model selection for AI-driven network design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00292v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Designing deployable and resilient network topologies from natural language requirements remains a challenging problem in network automation. This work investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate structurally valid and constraint-compliant network topologies through a constraint-driven pipeline combining hierarchical modeling and systematic validation. The framework is evaluated via a multimodel comparison of proprietary and open-weight LLMs across four realistic network scenarios released as a public dataset. We assess structural correctness using node and edge F1-scores against reference topologies, and evaluate resilience through server and content connectivity metrics. In addition, we analyze common failure modes, including interface mismatches and directional inconsistencies in generated topologies. Overall, this work provides a systematic benchmark for understanding how LLMs handle structural and resilience constraints in topology synthesis, and supports informed model selection for AI-driven network design.

items.title: Researchers introduce Rosetta, a composable native multimodal pretraining framework using Momentum-Anchored Orthogonal Projection to prevent catastrophic forgetting and enable seamless modality expansion [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Rosetta: Composable Native Multimodal Pretraining
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Rosetta, a new multimodal pretraining framework designed to integrate new data modalities without losing previously learned knowledge. Rosetta uses a modular approach that preserves core knowledge in shared components while allowing modality-specific features to be added through plug-and-play modules. This design addresses the problem of catastrophic forgetting common in existing architectures like Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT).

The framework introduces Momentum-Anchored Orthogonal Projection (MAOP), a technique that uses the optimizer's momentum to selectively block conflicting updates from new modalities while maintaining beneficial learning. Evaluations show that Rosetta maintains strong language and visual understanding, improves image generation, and enables effective cross-modal interactions. The researchers have made their code and models publicly available to support further advancements in multimodal AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.00293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Achieving true artificial general intelligence requires foundation models capable of integrating new modalities without forgetting prior knowledge. However, accommodating continuous generative objectives alongside discrete understanding tasks causes severe gradient conflicts. Existing architectures, including standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), are highly susceptible to representation overwriting. Even structurally partitioned paradigms like Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) remain vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting, severely impeding multimodal scalability. In this work, we introduce Rosetta, a composable native multimodal pretraining framework designed for seamless and non-destructive modality expansion. Rosetta adopts a modular paradigm where core foundational knowledge is preserved within global shared experts, while modality-specific capabilities are distributed across plug-and-play experts. To guarantee non-destructive composition, we propose Momentum-Anchored Orthogonal Projection (MAOP). MAOP leverages the optimizer's momentum state as an implicit semantic anchor, selectively neutralizing conflicting gradient components from new modalities while preserving synergistic updates. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that, while standard MoE and MoT architectures suffer catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge, Rosetta robustly preserves established language and visual understanding. Furthermore, it delivers superior image generation and unlocks cross-modal synergy, paving the way for truly composable and unified multimodal foundation models. To facilitate further multimodal research, we release our code and checkpoints to the community. Project page at https://rosetta-lmm.github.io/.
